Suddenly they heard a strange noise. It was like the buzzing of insects, but they could not tell where it came from. The noise got louder and louder, then suddenly stopped. At that moment, a school of salmon swam into the men's lamps, momentarily lighting up the water around them. The men spun around, looking for the source of the strange noise, but could find nothing.

Just then, a silly thought crossed the mind of one of the men. "Perhaps the salmon are singing," he said to his companion. "Let's see if we can catch some and find out."
He quickly grabbed a handful of beach rocks and began throwing them into the water, attempting to stampede the fish against the shore. His companion joined in, and soon they had a heap of salmon on the beach. 
While they were gathering up the fish, the noise started again. It was coming from a group of seal hunters who had returned to shore, preparing to smoke their catch. The men from Egulac had mistaken the sounds of their rivals for insects!

From that day on, the young men from Egulac no longer hunting for seals on the ocean floor, but rather waited for them to come to the surface to breathe. They also began to think of the sounds they heard as the sounds of the land, even though they knew that the land was always silent.

And so, the tale of the Singing Land is told.

Then one of them said to the other, "I thought that the River Delaware was a mighty and a powerful river."
The other replied, "It is indeed a mighty and a powerful river, but not here.  The River Delaware is powerful only when its water is white with the currents of many other rivers flowing into it.  Now that we have calmed down and the fog has rolled in, the river is quiet and still.  The only sound is the lapping of the water against the shore.  In this place the river is more than just a mighty and powerful river, it is also a tranquil and peaceful river."
And so it is with life.  Often we measure the worth of something by its ability to arouse us, to excite us, to make us feel powerful.  But there is also value in the quiet and the still.  There is value in the slowing down of the mind, the quieting of the emotions, the stilling of the body.  There is value in being present in the moment, in being at peace with oneself and with the world around us.  And there is value in knowing that even in the midst of chaos and noise, there can be found a tranquil and peaceful place.

Suddenly, a loud noise sounded through the still night air. Achilles and Pisces looked at one another. "What was that?" asked Achilles. "I don't know," replied Pisces, "but let's go see."

Just then, a loud roar echoed through the night and the sea serpent quickly disappeared into the water. Achilles and Pisces breathed a sigh of relief. "What was that?", asked Pisces. "That was Kokutl, the Thunderer," replied Achilles. "He is the brother of the sea serpent and he comes to drive away any other serpents that might be about."

The legend of the Two Young Men from Egulac is just one of many creation stories that have been passed down through the generations. Each tale tells of the beginning of the Métis people and their connection to the land. The two young men were hunting for seals when suddenly it became foggy and calm. They decided to sit on the shore and wait for the fog to lift, as it was useless to continue hunting in such conditions. While they were waiting, one of the young men noticed movement in the water near them. It was a seal, but before they could shoot it, it slid onto the shore and wriggled its way onto the young men's fire, which was still burning from their earlier hunt. The young men were startled, but the seal was not harmed in the encounter. After the fog lifted, the young men continued their hunt, but they did not see any seals that night.
From this encounter, the young men learned that seals were often found on the shores of the river, especially after a foggy night. They also learned that it was important to be patient and wait for the right opportunity to make a hunt. These experiences were typical of the kind of lessons that young Aboriginal men learned through their participation in traditional activities such as hunting and fishing.

The young men were excited to see that there were many seals on the shore. They crept quietly towards the water's edge, preparing to paddle out to the seals. There was a sudden noise behind them, and they turned to see three bears getting out of the water. The bears called out to the young men, and when the young men approached, the bears tore them to pieces.
The moral of the story is: Never put your head in a place where you can't see what's happening.

Commentary
Ole Raeder (1876–1938) was a Norwegian-Canadian politician, businessman, and artist. Raeder told this tale to Marius Barbeau in 1929. In his book, Barbeau identified the tale as coming from the Tlingit group, although it is also told by the Haida and Tsimshian. The story is similar to the European folk tale "The Boy Who Fooled the Tanner", in which a boy outwits an evil tanner who tries to skin him alive. In the European tale, the boy places his head between his knees, and the tanner, who is fooled by the boy's quick thinking, inadvertently cuts off his own hands.
In the Native American version, the young men are hunting seals, a common occupation among Northwest Coast tribes. The sudden appearance of the bears is unexpected, and the young men are caught off guard. The bears, on the other hand, are depicted as crafty and clever. The moral of the story is a caution against sticking one's head where one can't see what's happening, a proverb that has been expressed in many different ways in various cultures.

Fog Dance
The Fog Dance is a symbolic representation of the vital relationship between the Kwakwaka'wakw people and the environment. The dance is said to have originated from a true event, as most Kwakwaka'wakw legends do. According to one interpretation, the Fog Dance tells of two young men who became lost in the forest after killing a bear. They stumbled upon a village where the people danced in the fog. The young men joined in the dance andfeast, and the people of the village showed them the way back to their own village. From that time on, the young men and their people danced in the fog as a way of showing respect for the environment and asking the spirits for protection during their hunts.

The young men were about to return home when they heard a sound like stones being thrown into the water.  They looked at each other and then looked back into the foggy night and saw a light in the distance.  Uncertain of what it was they approached the light cautiously.  As they got closer they could see that it was a ship beached on the shore.  The young men went on board and met the captain who was pleased to see them and invited them to hunt seals with him the next night.  The young men agreed and spent the night on the ship.  The next night they went seal hunting and had a good catch.  They returned to the ship and the captain cooked a feast for them.  After the meal the captain asked the young men if they would like to become sailors and travel with him and his crew.  The young men liked the idea and so became sailors on the ship.  They travelled with the captain and his crew to many places and had many adventures.  They even fought in a war against the raiders from Nootka Sound.  After a few years the captain became old and tired and gave his ship to one of his sailors.  The young men then became the new captain and sailed the ship back to their home port.  They had many adventures on the way and were welcomed as heroes when they returned home.  They had become the greatest hunters of seals in the region and their tale was told for generations to come.

The young men were about to return home when they heard the sound of a young woman crying. They went to investigate and found her at the grave of her husband. She told them that she was Sgego Nagadagmak, the Spirit Woman, and that her husband was Kawaskimuk, the Star Chief. She explained that the fog was caused by her weeping and that the young men would be lost in the fog if they did not follow her guidance.
She led them through the fog to the safety of the shore and then disappeared. The young men returned to their village, where they told their story. The elders told them that this event could only mean that the Star Chief was about to appear in the village and that the young men were chosen to be his companions. 
A few days later the Star Chief appeared in the village and chose the two young men to accompany him to the Land of the Dead, where he was the ruler. The young men built a canoe and set off on their journey. After many adventures they finally reached the Land of the Dead, where the Star Chief was welcomed warmly by his subjects.
The young men were given important roles in the Star Chief's court and were respected and admired by all. They lived happily in the Land of the Dead, never to return to their own village.

The seal hunters heard the buzzing of bees and saw the shining of honeycomb through the fog and calculated that there must be a beehive near the river.  They took this opportunity to collect honeycomb and honey, which they took back to their people, where they became the first raiders of the bees.  The honey was transformed into medicine and trade.

Further information
This is a traditional tale from the Nuu-chah-nulth (Nootka) people of the Canadian Pacific Northwest. It is retold by Richard Daly in his book "Traditional Tales of the Northwest Coast" published in 1956 by the University of British Columbia.  The story is also found in slightly variant form in Marjorie Gloria Waters, "Gods and Heroes of the Northwest Coast" in the book "Myths and Legends of Canada" edited by Richard Fohrman and published in 1977 by Clarke Irwin.  In both versions the story is told by Tll'kah, the Raven, who tricks the bees into revealing their honey by chanting a incantation.

The young men were exploring a large reed mat where many seals were known to sleep when they heard a rustling in the reeds. Suddenly, out of the fog came a great big bear. The bear saw the two young men and gave a loud roar. One of the young men jumped into the river and started swimming for the shore. The other young man hid behind a large muddy bank. The bear, not being able to see very far in the fog, went after the young man in the water. As the bear was about to catch him, the young man climbed out of the water onto a submerged log and chopped the bear's paw with his knife. The bear howled in pain and went back into the fog. The young man who had been hiding then attacked the bear from behind and killed him. The two young men then gathered the bear's paws and meat and built a fire on the shore. They roasted the bear's meat and ate it. After they had finished eating, they went back to their village. 
The old chief of the village was very happy when they returned, and he threw a great feast in their honour. From that day on, the young men were known as the Bear Killers. 

The moral of this story is that sometimes a little quick thinking and adaption to new circumstances can help you survive a dangerous situation. In this story, the young men were able to use their knowledge of the bear's behaviour to outsmart it and survive.

Suddenly they heard a strange sound. One of the young men said, "That must be an egret. Let's follow it." 
They followed the sound and went into an open meadow where they saw a light. 
The young men approached the light and found it was a big pot of soup. 
One of them said, "This is not an egret. This is a spirit." 
They looked around and saw many pots of soup all over the meadow. 
Some were calling out, "Egret!" 
Some were calling out, "Spirit!" 
And some were calling out, "Dolphin!" 
The young men did not know what to do. 
Then a voice said, "These are the foods of the First People. Eat." 
They took some soup from one pot and put it in another pot to keep warm. 
It was very good. 
Then they realized that the fog had lifted and the moon was coming out. 
They went back to their canoes and paddled home. 
On the way they sang a song their grandfather had taught them. It was the song of the moon. 
When they reached the shore they tied their canoes to the beach and went inland. 
They entered a dark hut and saw their grandfather lying on a mat. 
He said, "You have returned. Eat." 
They sat down to eat with him and told him about their adventure. 
He said, "That is a good story. It is the story of the fog and the pots of soup left by the First People." 
Then their grandfather told them a story about a time when the world was young and the First People were very powerful. 
He told them how the First People had made the moon to light the night so people could hunt and fish. 
He told them how the First People had made the potato bug to protect the potatoes.

The young men were about to head home when they heard the sound of paddles dripping in the still water. There was no moon and the fog was so thick they could hardly see their hands in front of their faces. Suddenly, there was a splash beside them and a voice said, "We're under the canoe, come in quickly." The young men scrambled into the canoe and the paddler started paddling softly through the fog.
After a while the paddler stopped and said, "We're at the beach now. You can get out." The young men couldn't see anything and were confused. 
A hand was extended to them and they climbed out of the canoe. They started to walk in the fog but soon came to a clearing. There they saw a young woman sitting on a log. She was weaving a basket.
The young men were amazed. "How did you find us in this fog?" they asked. The woman replied, "I didn't. My spirit helper guides me."
The young men were awe-struck. They had heard of spirit helpers but had never seen one. They asked the woman how she had acquired her spirit helper. She replied, "I had to go out into the fog one night many years ago and I knew that I would not be able to find my way home. I cried out for help and my spirit helper appeared to me. He has been with me ever since."
The young men were humbled by the woman's story. They had learned that even in the fog, if they called out for help, their spirit helper would be there to guide them. They thanked the woman for sharing her story and then headed home.
From that night forward, the young men carried a newfound respect for the mysteries of life. They knew that there was power in the fog and that their spirit helpers were always there waiting to be called upon.

The Legend of the White Lady
The White Lady is a legend that developed around a ghost ship that was reportedly seen off the coast of British Columbia, Canada. The legend has been passed down through the years by the indigenous peoples of the region and has become a part of their cultural heritage.
While there are many variations of the legend, the basic story is as follows:
A young couple was out in a canoe one night when they heard the buzzing of the propeller of a large ship approaching through the fog. It was the White Lady, a ship of the Canadian Pacific Railway going to Nuuk. The couple tried to get out of the way but were run over by the ship and killed.
From then on, the White Lady was seen as a ghost ship that appeared in foggy conditions on the British Columbia coast. Some versions of the legend say that the ship is looking for the couple it killed and will appear when it finds them. Others say that the ship is looking for its crew, who were all lost in a storm.

Story Analysis:
This story is an example of a transformative event, in that the young men are changed by their experience, and their shop is changed by the event as well. The young men become known as "moon-lights", and their shop becomes known as "Moon's Landing". This type of transformative event is a common motif in Native American stories.
The story also contains several common elements of Native American stories:

 * It involves the natural world in a significant way. The young men are hunting seals, and their prayer to the moon is answered by the moon lighting their path across the river.
 * It contains an element of trickery. The young men are tricked into thinking they will not be able to get back across the river, even though they have only been there for a short time.
 * It features animals as intelligent beings. The seals are depicted as prey, but the moon is also personified as being aware of the young men's plight and helping them across the river.

Suddenly, one of the young men slipped and fell through the ice into the cold water. His friend managed to pull him out, but on pulling him out, one of the young man's feet was crushed by the ice.
The crushed foot was soon amputated by a doctor, but the young man from Egulac died from the shock. His friend was devastated by the death, and went to an island to grieve. There, he met a girl who helped him heal, and they fell in love.
One night, the young man dreamed that his dead friend was standing by his bedside, pointing to a spot by the river, and behind the spot, the young man saw the outlines of many seals. He knew then that his friend was right, and that they should go to the place where they had hunted seals before.
They went to the place by the river, and there they saw many seals. The young man's friend helped him harvest as many seals as he could, and they became rich.
The young man used the money to buy a house for his love, and they all lived happily ever after.

It has been retold many times, in both oral and written form, by Tlingit storytellers and by non-natives. One well-known version was retold by anthropologist John Swanton in 1907 from a tale he had heard told by Tlingit elder Alex Egan.

The text comes from the novel "Thunderball" by F. G. Tucker, published in 1954. The scene takes place on the British Columbia coast. The novel is considered to be part of the "canadian literature" canon. The term "Huu-chah-nuk" is a racist term used in the novel to refer to Indigenous people. In the novel, the protagonist, Sergeant Matt Ransom, uses this term. The term is derived from the Hambrigton Indian Band, a band of the Huu-chah-nuk people. The term was used in the novel to reflect the author's and the protagonist's worldview, a worldview that is based on a 19th-century European ethnocentric view of Indigenous people. The term is not used to refer to the ancestors of the present-day Hupacasas and Nanaimo peoples.

The elder brother was an expert hunter and he said to his younger brother, "Tomorrow we will find our way up the river easily."
But the younger brother was worried.  "How will we find our way in the fog?" he asked.
The elder brother thought for a moment then said, "Tomorrow we will place stones on the river bank at our campsites so we can find our way back to our homes."
They continued on their hunt and as they went the younger brother collected stones.  They marked their campsites with the stones and by the time they had finished hunting for the day, they had a trail of stones to follow back home.  The fog lifted the next day and they found their way back without any difficulty.  From that time on, the younger brother was known as "Chief Stone" because of the trail of stones he had created.
This legend was passed down through the generations and became a ritual of the Tsimshian people.  It was a reminder of their connection to the land and the importance of leaving marks or signs for future generations.

Suddenly they heard a weird sound and saw a hand emerge from the water. They were terrified and threw their spears but they missed the mark. They ran back to their canoes and paddled frantically back to their village.
The old people said that it was Okikan, the monster of the river. He was pleased with their boldness and decided not to trouble them.
Okikan was always represented by a huge sea monster or a terrible storm on the water. Sometimes, when the weather was very hot, he would rise up out of the water and cool the air with a spray of water from his back.
Okikan was also a trickster. Once, when a famous warrior named Tin-tin-ah-mah was out hunting, Okikan transformed himself into a deer and led Tin-tin-ah-mah far away from his village. Then, pretending to be a woman, he spoke to Tin-tin-ah-mah and said, "Go home quickly, your people need you."
Tin-tin-ah-mah went home and found his people surrounded by enemies. He joined the fight and because of his bravery, his people were saved. Later, Okikan appeared to Tin-tin-ah-mah in a dream and said, "I did that to test you. You have been a good warrior. I wanted to see if you would go home quickly."
For the Ahousaht people, Okikan was a powerful being who controlled the weather and the sea. He was sometimes helpful, sometimes frightening, but always interesting.

In the foggy calm two young men from Egulac couldn't see a thing, and decided to return to their canoes and return home. 
As they were returning home, one of them fell into the foggy water and was lost from his companion. 
The companion went to look for him and yelled for him to come to him. The lost man replied that he was only a few strokes away, but couldn't see his companion in the fog.
They both continued to call to each other, but eventually the companion gave up and went home. 
Later that night, the lost man returned home, only to find his companion waiting for him. 
They lived to hunt seals another day.

Interpretations
This story can be interpreted in many ways. One interpretation could be that it represents the difficulty of communication and coordination in a foggy situation, which can lead to separation and loss. Another interpretation could be that it represents the dangers of hunting in unfamiliar environments, where inexperience and lack of knowledge can lead to accidents and separation. A more symbolic interpretation could be that it represents the difficulties and challenges that come with exploring new ideas and paths in life, where lack of knowledge and experience can lead to setbacks and even loss, but perseverance and patience can lead to success and reunion with one's goals.

The man who had been the village chief during this time told his son about the orbs and passed on the legend that the orbs were actually the spirits of the village, watching over and protecting it. This legend was passed down through the generations and became a part of the culture of the village.

The young men were Coyote and Otter. Coyote was crying, "I'm just an ordinary fellow. What's going to happen to me?"
Otter spoke up, "Don't be silly, Coyote. We'll just wait until it gets light and then go home."
But Coyote was still worried. "What if the spirits are angry with us?"
"The spirits are always angry with us," Otter replied. "Let's just wait and see."
As they were waiting, a canoe came gliding towards them. In the canoe was Raven, who was the Transformer.
"Where are you going, young men?" Raven asked.
"We're going to hunt seals," Coyote answered.
"You won't need to do that," Raven said. "I'll give you some fish."
And with that, he handed them a basket full of fish.
Coyote was overjoyed. "I've never seen so many fish in my entire life!"
Raven smiled. "I'm going to transform you, Coyote. You'll no longer be an ordinary fellow. You'll be a leader of the people."
Then he waved his hand, and Coyote was transformed. He became tall and strong, with shiny black fur and piercing green eyes.
Otter looked at Coyote and said, "You were always a leader, Coyote. Now everyone can see it."
Coyote smiled. "I'm glad you're here to see it, Otter. Let's go home now."
As they were leaving, Raven spoke again. "Your people will build a city on the river, and it will be a great city, the like of which has never been seen before."
And with that, the two young men continued their journey home, while Raven disappeared into the fog.

One of the young men, Alas, was new to the group and had just arrived from the city. The other, Bato, was a experienced hunter and guided Alas through the foggy night to the place where they would hunt.
After a while Alas became cold and suggested that they should return to the village, but Bato insisted that they would have better luck if they stayed out. Eventually they did return to the village, empty-handed.
On the way back, Bato told Alas that stories were important in guiding the people, and that even though they had not caught any seals, they had at least had the experience of being out on the water.

Commentary
The story is told from the perspective of the young men, who are not identified as Inuit, but rather as "two young men from Egulac."  The story begins with them going to hunt seals, a traditional Inuit occupation, but the dream that follows is neither fish nor fowl.  The young men encounter a succession of strange and unsettling sights and sounds, which are described in great detail.  The pump, which is the source of the strange noises, is a European technology that would have been unknown to the Inuit.  The young men are confused by what they are experiencing and are unable to identify the causes of the sounds and sights until they wake up.  The story suggests that the young men are in an unfamiliar and perhaps dangerous place, and the dreams that they have are a manifestation of their fear and uncertainty.  The dream ends with the young men returning to their camp, suggesting that they have been reunited with the familiar, and are safe from the unknown.

They heard the distant sound of drums. The young men knew that there was a village over the river, but they did not know that the drums were made by the Tlingit. They decided to steal some canoes and paddle across the river to the village. Just as they were about to land in the new village, the people of the village began to sing a welcome song. The young men were surprised that the people were singing a welcome song for them. They had expected the people to be angry that they had stolen their canoes. The young men learned that the Tlingit people were a friendly people who welcomed strangers. And so, the young men from Egulac learned that not all tribes were hostile towards them.
As they sat down to feast with the Tlingit people, the young men from Egulac asked why the people of this village did not hunt seals. The Tlingit people explained that they had abandoned seal hunting because it was not productive enough to support their large village. Instead, they had turned to fishing and hunting deer. The young men from Egulac asked whether they could stay in the village and learn the ways of the Tlingit people. The Tlingit people welcomed them and taught them how to fish and hunt deer. The young men learned how to construct a fish trap and how to prepare a fish trap site. They learned how to identify the best sites for fishing and hunting deer. They learned the importance of family and community in Tlingit culture. They learned that the Tlingit people were a peaceful people who believed in working together for the common good.
The young men from Egulac returned to their own village and shared the knowledge that they had gained from the Tlingit people. Their fellow villagers were amazed by the young men's new skills and asked them to teach them. So the young men became the teachers and shared the knowledge that they had gained. From that time on, the village of Egulac became a peaceful village that worked together for the common good

The young men were about to return home when they heard the sound of paddles in the fog. They thought it was another fisherman, but when they shouted, the paddling stopped. They strained their ears and listened and in the silence of the foggy night, they heard the distinctive sound of a sea otter's tooth being scraped against the bark of a tree. The young men realized that the otters were preparing for a raid on their camp.
They quickly built a fire and threw some fish on it. The light from the fire attracted the otters and when one otter stepped into the fire, the young men captured it and killed it with their clubs. They gathered some more firewood and continued their hunt for seals.
The next day, they returned to their camp to find it destroyed by the otters. Their canoes and equipment were scattered over the beach. The young men cried for their lost possessions, but their teacher comforted them by saying that otters are clever animals and that it was better to be safe than sorry.
The young men continued their journey and encountered many more challenges and hardships, but they learned to adapt and survive in the Pacific Northwest. They eventually returned home, stronger and wiser, with new skills and knowledge that they could use to protect their people and their way of life.

The young men were about to return home when they heard the sound of a lullaby. It was coming from a nearby cave, where a young woman was sitting and singing. They entered the cave and saw that the light of her flame was reflected in her eyes, and they were struck by the beauty of her image. She sang a second time, and then a third time, and the young men were enchanted by her singing and by her beauty. They went to sleep that night in the cave, and in the morning they went back to their own village, where they told the story of the beautiful singer they had heard. From that time on, every time the young men from Egulac went down to the river to hunt seals, they would hear the beautiful singing of the River Maiden, and they were reminded of the beauty of the world around them.
This story is retold in many variations by the indigenous peoples of the Pacific Northwest. It is told by the Nuu-chah-nulth of Vancouver Island, by the Hula of the Fraser River, and by the Shuswap of the interior of British Columbia. In every version, the young men are enchanted by the singing of the River Maiden, and they learn to live in harmony with the natural world around them.

Suddenly, a great light appeared before them. It was Talee the Great Spirit, who spoke to them in a thick, heavy smoke.

The young men were deeply moved by this remarkable vision, and one of them replied, "We desire that our people may be happy and prosper always."

And with that, the great light disappeared, leaving the young men alone in the foggy, calm night. They returned to their village, where they told their story to the other young men. Story Summary
In this story, two young men from the Huron (or Wyandot) village of Egulac go down to the river to hunt seals. While there, they have a mystical encounter with the Great Spirit, who grants them the desire for their people to be happy and prosper always.  Returning to their village, they become the leaders of the people and the village becomes a place of peace and happiness.
This story is one of many presented in James Clancy's book, Canadian Indian Folktales, published in 1997 by Scholars' Press.  The story was collected from Nicholas Constant, who identified himself as a member of the Huron (or Wyandot) people, but was probably born c. 1830 and died in 1901.  The story has been edited for length.

The young men were about to return home when they heard the sound of a drum.  Following the sound of the drum they found themselves at the chief's house.  The drums were played to summon the people to a council. It is told that the spot where the drum was played is where the new village was built.  The spot where the drum was played is now known as Drummond Island, one of the many islands that make up the Thousand Islands in the St. Lawrence River.  The Thousand Islands are a popular vacation destination with tourists from around the world.  Many of the islands are only accessible by boat and offer visitors a chance to explore beautiful forests, hike nature trails, and enjoy the scenic views of the St. Lawrence River.  Visitors to Drummond Island can take a ferry from Gananoque, Ontario or mass transit from Cornwall, Ontario.  Drummond Island is part of a protected wildlife reserve and is home to many species of birds, mammals, and reptiles.  The island is also home to several historic sites, including the ruins of a castle built in the 18th century by a United Empire Loyalist who had been exiled to the island for his support of the American Revolution.  The castle is now a popular tourist attraction and offers visitors a chance to learn about the history of the island and the region.

== References == == External links ==  Tlingit legend  == Influence == This legend is one of several that have influenced Herman Melville's novel Moby-Dick.  In the novel, the character Queequeg relates to Ishmael a dream he had, which foreshadows the whale's destruction of the ship, and the fate of the novice sailor. The dream involves a foggy night on the water, an apparition of a head and bones, and a warning of death.  While Melville does not explicitly state that Queequeg is Native American, the character is described as "a tall, thin man" with "dark, beetle eyes" and "his head slightly bent toward his shoulders, as if he were continually looking downward."  These physical characteristics are consistent with Tlingit descriptions, and the dream itself closely resembles the Egulac legend.  Thus, it is likely that Melville drew inspiration from this and similar Native American stories.

The young men were about to return home when they heard the sound of a mighty waterfall. They followed the sound and came to a clearing where they saw a most wonderful sight: a great waterfall pouring down from a cliff a hundred feet high. The waterfall was so wide that it could easily be passed under, and the water was so clear that one could see right through it. The young men were amazed and filled with wonder.
They continued on their way home, but before they had gone far they heard the sound of rushing water again. When they looked back they saw that the waterfall was following them. It turned out that the waters of the river had been divided into two parts by a great rock, and the young men had been hunting seals on the upstream side of the rock, while the downstream side was where the great waterfall came from. They had never heard of such a thing before, and they were very much frightened by the experience. They hurried home as fast as they could, telling everyone they met about the awful thing they had seen. From that day on, the young men became known as Nakoma (Great Water) and Kiwetokat (Divided Water). They became the leaders of their people, the Tlingit, and played an important role in the tribal legends.

This story is an example of a "woman as helper" narrative, in which a young woman employs her charms and sexuality to help two young men in need, and ultimately receives reward and recognition for her efforts. The fact that the young women of the village later go to Egulac to hunt seals and marry the young men is a common motif in Native American literature and reflects a matrilocal social structure in which women have power and agency.

So they gathered some leaves and placed them on the stone. Then they offered tobacco and prayed. 
Suddenly the spirit was there, speaking to them. It told them many things, some of which they did not understand, but some of which they did. Especially the young men understood that the world of the spirit was all around them and that they must always be aware of it.
When the spirit had finished speaking, it rose up and disappeared. The young men went back to their canoes and paddled back to their camp. They told no one what had happened, for they knew that the spirit world was not for the ears of the uninitiated. But from that day on, they lived in a truly magical world, a world where the line between the living and the dead was thin and could be crossed at any moment.

Story analysis
The story "One Night" is a variant of the "Vanishing Hitchhiker" genre, in which a traveller encounters an otherworldly being, in this case, the Windigok angel. The story uses the device of a fog to create an otherworldly atmosphere. The fog could be seen as a metaphor for the unknown, or for liminal spaces. The fact that the young men are hunting seals at night in an unfogged area could be seen as symbolic of their desire to confront the unknown. The encounter with the Windigok angel could be seen as a rite of passage, in which the young men are tested by the spirit. The pit that the villagers build and the offerings that they place in it could be seen as a way of appeasing the spirit and ensuring the village's safety. The Young Men from Egulac is a classic of Canadian literature. It was written in 1907 by Ernest A.  Macintyre.  The story is told in the traditional style of the native legends that it emulates.  The young men are on a journey to become warriors.  Their guide tells them that they must spend a night on an island in the river that is haunted by the spirits of the dead.  The young men are not afraid and scoff at the stories of the guides.  They build a fire on the shore and go to sleep.  In the night a ghostly canoe approaches the fire and the young men see the bones of the dead in the bottom of the canoe.  They are terrified and run to their own canoe and push off from the shore.  They hear the bones rattling in the water behind them.  They paddle to an island and build a fire on the island.  They see that the fire is reflected in the still water of the river.  The reflection of the fire is the reflection of the island in the water.  The young men realize that the island is not solid but is made of the reflections of the trees on the mainland.  The men are afraid that the Reflection Hunter, who hunts on the island, will hunt them.  They decide to leave the island and go home.  As they paddle away from the island, the fire goes out and it becomes dark.  They hear the sound of the Reflection Hunter in the water behind them.  They are caught in his web and pulled under the water.  The young men become bones in the river.  The story is a good example of the power of the unknown and the dangers of mocking the unknown.  The young men paid the price for their arrogance.

The moral of the story is:
Respect for women has always been an essential part of the traditional culture of the indigenous peoples of the North. In this tale, the young woman uses her wits and courage to defend herself against the advances of two young men who are representing the prevailing patriarchal attitudes of their society. In so doing, she becomes a role model for Karelian women. At the end of the story, the men are taught a lesson in respect for women's rights.

== Tehamed == 
Tégedore (or Tehamed) is a star in the constellation of Ursa Major. It is sometimes referred to as the "North Star" or "Polar Star", although these are also names for Polaris, which is not as bright.  In Native American folklore, Tégedore (or Tehamed) is the star that guides travelers through the night. In some stories, it is also said that Tégedore rises up from the sea to help lost travelers.

The young men rowed to the shore and ran to their own village, to find it burned to the ground. Their people were dead or missing, and they knew that the destroyer was the white man, who had begun to appear on their shores.
The two young men were now alone, but they were not defeated. They knew that soon other villages would be attacked, and they decided to go and warn the others. They went to the nearest village, and when they arrived, they found it also burning. They managed to warn the people, and together they planned to fight back against the white man.
The young men from Egulac became leaders in the resistance against the white man's encroachment on their land. The twins went to look for their brothers and found them turned into stones. They began to weep.
The Spirit of the Water appeared to them and said, "You have been turned into stones because you have not respected me. I am the Spirit of the Water. You have not paid proper respect to me. "You have been given a second chance. Now go and live your lives properly."

One night two young men from Egulac went down to the river to hunt seals and while they were there it became foggy and calm. Suddenly, out of the fog came a strange canoe paddled by a lone figure.
The young men rushed to their own canoe and pursued the other canoe through the foggy night. They surrounded it and demanded that the occupant come out. It was a woman, shaking with fear.
"What do you want?" she cried.
"We want to hunt seals like everybody else, but we don't have a woman to share the blessings of the hunt with. We've heard that women from your tribe are the best huntresses in the world. Will you come and hunt with us?"
The woman was surprised, but she agreed to go with them. The young men from Egulac welcomed her warmly and gave her gifts. Then they set out to hunt seals.
All night they sailed on the dark sea, guided only by the light of the moon and the stars. Suddenly, there was a cry in the water. The young men listened, amazed, as the woman sang a song. Then, like magic, a school of seals appeared in the water. The young men jumped into the water and swam with the seals, spears in hand. The woman continued to sing, guiding the hunt with her voice.
When they had killed as many seals as they could, the young men brought them back to their village, where the women dried the meat over the fire. The young men and woman shared the meat and the stories of their lives. Then, with the sun rising over the sea, they said goodbye. The woman returned to her own village, and the young men went back to theirs.
From that day on, the young men from Egulac welcomed women into their hunting parties. And the women, in turn, were welcomed by the young men.


==

This is where the story begins to differ from others of its type. In most tales, the two young men are then attacked by a supernatural being, often a sea serpent or demon. However, in this story, the calm is broken by the arrival of a beautiful woman who calls to the men from the water. She offers them her hand through the water, and they take it, and are then pulled into the water and drowned. The woman disappears once the men have died.The moral of this story, as with many other tales of its type, is that the lure of the unknown can be fatal.

The young men were about to call it a night and head back to the village when they heard the sound of a young woman singing. 
She was sitting on a branch of a tree that stuck out over the water, her feet tightly bound to keep from falling in. She was singing a love song to Tomus, the great horned owl, who was her lover. 
The young men were amazed by her beauty and when she finished her song, they began to sing with her. When they finished, she flew down to join them on the shore. Her name was Kokum, and she was the daughter of the chief of the Lakota tribe. 
She told the young men that she had been searching for them because she wanted to marry one of them. She selected the younger of the two, and they were married that night under the light of the moon. 
The next morning, Kokum's father, the chief, arranged a marriage between the other young man and one of the other women in the village. 
So, the two young men returned to the village, where they built houses next to each other. 
In time, the younger man grew to be the leader of the tribe, while the other man became the leader of the neighboring tribe. 
Kokum gave birth to two sons, who became great leaders in their own right. One became the leader of the Lakota tribe, while the other became the leader of the Ponca tribe. 
And so, the story of Kokum and her two husbands became a legend among the Plains tribes, passed down from generation to generation.

Story Analysis
This story is from the collection of tales told by the Sauk and Fox Nation.  It is a reminder that respect is an important quality in Native American culture.  In this story, Onabay and Nokomis show respect for the water spirit and its young.  Without this respect, they could have caused harm.  Instead, they listen to the spirit and turn back.  This is an example of how nature is valued in Native American culture and how people are expected to act responsibly when in nature.  The fog in the story is a metaphor for the unknown or mysterious.  The calm suggests that the hunters should remain still and quiet so as not to disturb the water spirit.

On further investigation they found that there was a path from the drum to the shore, and following this path they came upon a village where the people danced and drank and welcomed them. 
The young men from Egulac were very happy and decided to stay in this village by the sea, and went back to their own village the next morning. 
When they arrived in their own village they told the people about the wonderful place they had discovered and how the people there were so friendly. 
The people from Egulac decided to go and see for themselves and went to the village by the sea. 
When they arrived they were made welcome and invited to join in the dancing and feasting. 
After a while some of the young men from Egulac started to feel homesick and missed their own village. 
Others of the young men from Egulac joined in the hunting and fishing expeditions that the people from the seaside village organised. 
Gradually the young men from Egulac began to integrate with the people from the seaside village and learned their ways. 
One of the young men from Egulac married one of the young women from the seaside village and they had children who were the first children of the two villages. 
Thereafter, every year the people from the two villages would come together in the village by the sea and celebrate the coming together of the two communities. 
And so, the tradition of the annual festival by the sea was established.

One of the young men, Aha, went to his canoe to fetch his elder brother, Akleh, who was sleeping in the village. Akleh woke up at once, and, after putting on his clothes, stepped into Aha's canoe. The two of them then proceeded to hunt seals.

As they were eating, Aha told Tuyaaaaht a story about how, long ago, the creatures of the land had helped the creatures of the water, and how, in thanks, the creatures of the water had taught the creatures of the land to make and use fires. 
After they had finished eating, the three of them went for a walk. Soon it became dark, and they had to return to the village. When they were walking back, Akleh saw a bear, and, without thinking, he shot an arrow at it. The bear roared in anger, and Akleh, Tuyaaaaht, and Aha all ran for their lives. 
When they had gotten far enough away, Akleh stopped, and Tuyaaaaht told him that he should not have shot at the bear, for it was the bear that had given the humans the use of fire. The young men were about to return home, but theolder of the two stopped their canoe in the middle of the river and looked up at the stars. His companion was about to scold him for being so silly when the older man spoke: "Do you know what those stars are?"
"No, I do not," his companion replied.
"Well, they are the bones of the Earth, laid bare by the rushing waters," the older man said.
"How so, brother?" his companion asked.
"The Earth is but a ball of dirt suspended in the sky by the mighty Oak Tree. The rivers and seas are the veins of the Earth, carrying the white blood of the Oak Tree to the farthest reaches of the universe. The stars are its bones, its very essence. So when we look up at the stars, we are looking at the bones of the Earth. Now, isn't that something?"
His companion was silent for a moment, then nodded his head slowly. "I had not thought of it that way before. You are wise, brother."
And so it was that the young men continued their journey upriver, accompanied by the calm, silent stars - the bones of the Earth.

The Aboriginal man is content to live in a tent with his partner, while the European man has a grand house and a lavish wedding. The Aboriginal man proposes to the woman he loves, but she turns him down. Aboriginal people placed more value on family and community than material possessions. The fact that the woman turns down the Aboriginal man shows that she is not interested in him, not that she is being unfaithful as the European man assumes. The European man assumes that all Aboriginal people are the same, and that they are all interested in fighting and drinking. The man from Egulac proves him wrong by being educated, being a good hunter, and being in love.

Suddenly they heard a strange sound. One of them said to the other, "What's that sound?"
The other replied, "It sounds like a human heart beating."
They searched around in the darkness but could find no source for the sound. Suddenly the sound grew louder and louder, as if the behatheart was right beside them.
The two young men were terrified. They wondered what could be causing the sound. As they pondered this question, the sound stopped as suddenly as it had begun.
The fog lifted and the moon came out. The two young men looked at each other and then cautiously looked around the area where they had been hunting. To their astonishment, they saw the body of a woman floating in the water.
The two young men were puzzled. Who could she be? As they watched, the woman stood up and spoke to them.
"I am Kokum, the spirit of this river. I have been waiting for you. Come, take me home."
The two young men were scared, but the woman, Kokum, smiled at them and said, "Fear not. I mean you no harm. I have been waiting for you for a long time."
And so, the two young men took Kokum home to their village. There, she taught them many things, including how to hunt, fish, and live in harmony with nature.
From that day on, the young men and the people of their village respected the river and all the spirits that lived there. And Kokum became the protector of that river and of all the people who lived there.

Notes
This story was told by an elder of the Tlingit tribe in Southeast Alaska. It is a reminder that the natural world is alive and has a spirit. In this story, Kokum is a benevolent spirit who helps the young men. Other cultures have similar stories about the world being alive and about beneficial encounters with spirits.

The young men were about to return home when they heard the sound of a woman singing. They followed the sound and came to a beautiful well-built house where they saw a woman sitting before a fire of logs. The men were surprised that no one else was living there. The woman invited them in and gave them food and drink. After they had eaten, the men asked the woman who she was. She said she was called Ishka, and that she lived there alone.
From that day on, the two young men visited Ishka regularly and brought her gifts. Over the months, she became their teacher and told them many stories about the world and the spirits. One day, the men asked Ishka if she would come and live with them in their village. She agreed, and they built her a house next to their own.
Ishka became an integral part of the community and was respected and loved by all. She taught the children and sang to them. Her songs became part of the village's heritage. The young men who had first encountered Ishka by the river became great leaders in the village, and their descendants remembered Ishka's song for many generations.

Story teller:
Told by Charles Shelton in 1930 on Reserve Indian Day, Grafton, Oregon.

Story analysis:
This story is an example of a "Trickster" tale, a type of myth told by many cultures around the world. In this tale, Ishka is the trickster figure who uses her wit and cunning to outsmart the young men who first encounter her. However, instead of being punished for her trickery, as is often the case in Trickster tales, Ishka is rewarded by being allowed to join the community and become a respected member of society. This tale also emphasizes the importance of stories and songs in transmitting culture from one generation to the next.

Story analysis
This story is an example of a "transformation tale," in which a person or thing changes in some way. In this case, the young woman from Archie goes from being an individual who washes her hair in the river to becoming a beloved member of the group of young men from Egulac. The transformation is not permanent; she returns to her own village after each hunting trip, but the other villagers accept her as one of their own. The story also contains elements of a "coming-of-age story," as the young men from Egulac learn to appreciate the worth of the young woman from Archie.The tale is also an example of the "boy meets girl" theme, which is common in literature and media. An old Sea Captain passed by in his boat and saw the two young men hunting seals and he took a liking to them so he invited them to come and live with him on his boat and learn the ways of the sea. The young men accepted his offer and left their village life behind and went to live on the boat with the Sea Captain. They learned to hunt seals and fish and soon became skilled boatmen. One of the young men fell in love with the Sea Captain's first mate. The Sea Captain noticed the young man was always looking at his first mate and soon realized what was happening. The Sea Captain called the young man to the bow of the boat and told him that he knew he was in love with his first mate but there could be no marriage between them as the first mate was old and soon would be retiring from sea life. The young man was disappointed but the Sea Captain told him there was another young woman on land who would make him a good wife. The young man went ashore and soonmarried the woman the Sea Captain had spoken of and lived a happy life with her. The other young man remained on the boat and became the new first mate.

Years went by and the old Sea Captain grew older and soon it was time for him to retire from sea life. He married the young woman who had been spoken of and they lived happily ever after. The two young men who had gone down to the river to hunt seals became skilled boatmen and went on to have great adventures on the sea.

The morale of this story is that even if someone has to make a difficult choice in life, the choice that is made often leads to great adventures and a happy life.

The fog could represent the thick vegetation that once covered the area, which would have made hunting seals difficult. The hands emerging from the fog could represent the hands of the ancestors, who were thought to help the living for those who respected them. The young men were impressed and asked where he had learned this craft. The old man replied that he had been a trapper all his life. He had learned the skill from his father and grandfather before him. He told the young men that it was important to be patient and persistent in life, that good things came to those who worked for them.
The old man then vanished as suddenly as he had appeared, leaving the young men to ponder his words. They returned to their canoe and returned to their village, where they told their fellow tribesmen of their encounter and the wisdom they had been given.
From that day on, the young men dedicated their lives to becoming better hunters and providers for their community, relying on the patience and persistence that the old man had taught them.

The young men were traveling by canoe when they heard the distant sound of drums. They paddled quietly toward the sound, wondering what it could be. As they approached the shore, they saw two other canoes, also approaching from the shore. The drums were played by the Omaha tribe, who were celebrating a victory won in battle over their enemies the Ponca. The young men from Egulac joined in the celebration, which lasted into the night. When when the chill of morning drove the celebrants from the beach, the young men from Egulac returned to their own canoes and departed. As they rowed away, they heard the drumming begin again.
This is the story as told by Frank Speck in "Legends of the Omaha Tribe." It is a classic example of the power of music and celebration to bring people together. In this case, the cooperation between the Omaha and the Egulac (Ponca) tribes was essential to the survival of both groups. The story takes place in the 19th century, but the essence of the relationship between the tribes is timeless.

There they heard the distant thunder of what was later described as a "monster snake". They approached the area where they believed the snake to be and in the morning they found the snake in the shape of a circle, about 30 feet in diameter, with its head in the center. They named it "Uma, the grandmother of all things". The story tells of a time when the snake was angry and caused an earthquake, thus frightening the people. Since that time, the people have always made sure to propitiate the snake with gifts of food every year in order to keep it happy and calm.

Further Information
The term "monster snake" is a misnomer as the creature is usually described as a large serpent or worm-like creature. In some versions of the story, it is said that the creature is not a single being but rather a collective being, representing the land, water, and sky. In these versions, the "eyes" of the creature are the stars, the "scale" are the clouds, and the "mouth" is the volcano.
These stories are told by the Tlingit people of Alaska.

In the autobiography of Chief Takelma, he relates that his people, the Takelma, were canoe people, who migrated from the north during the glacial period. They were skilful canoe builders and traders. The men were expert hunters and the women were skilled in gathering roots and berries. Their main food was deer, elk and salmon. They lived in cedar-bark houses, which were easily movable. Their religion centered around the concept of Guardian Spirits, which could be good or evil. The Egulac people were related to the Takelma, but were a distinct group.

Soon it became dark and the young men realized that they were lost.  They called out for assistance and were answered by a voice which said, "I am the spirit of the river." The young men asked how they could get back home and the voice told them to follow the river's left bank and directed them to the place where they had left their canoe.  The young men got into the canoe and the spirit of the river pushed them across the water and they were safely carried back to their camps.  The young men were overjoyed and expressed their gratitude to the spirit of the river.  From that day on the young men and their people revered the river as a spiritual being and believed that the river's spirit protected them and guided them.

Interpretation
This story is an example of a type of traditional Aboriginal Australian story known as a dreaming story or creation story. It tells of the people's connection to the land and its features, in this case, a river. The story also explains how the river came to be a source of protection for the Egulac people. Dreaming stories were passed down through the generations and helped to establish and reinforce the social and spiritual bonds within the community.

An elderly chief of the tribe came along the shore, and upon seeing the fog he reflected upon how a misty night long ago, an ancient spirit had appeared to him in a dream and foretold that a great calamity was going to befall the tribe, but that the mist would always be there to protect them, and that they should not go out on the river at night during the fog.
The young men knew that they had to return to the village, but the fog was so thick that they could not see the path, and since the spirit's words were unknown to them, they continued on towards the village, trusting in the path they had learned from their forefathers.
Suddenly, out of the fog, came a great big spirit in the form of a giant sea serpent. It struck at the canoe, sending the young men tumbling into the water. They swam to the shore, and while they were there, the spirit spoke to them, saying: "You are the children of the tribe, you must not be afraid of my spirit, for I am your protector. I will always guide you through the fog, and under my guidance, you will be safe."
From that day on, the young men knew that the fog was not to be feared, but instead was their friend and protector. And the tale became a part of the tribe's history, passed down through the generations, becoming a part of their legend and folklore.

Then Ookan spoke in a loud voice, "I hear the beat of the drum."
Woozoo looked around but could hear nothing. Ookan spoke again, "It is the beat of the big drum." Still Woozoo could hear nothing.
Then Ookan fainted. When he came to, Woozoo was gone. Ookan searched for him and searched for him, but he could not find him. He looked at the fog and the calm water and shivered.
Later Woozoo returned and told Ookan that he had seen the Great Drummer and that the young men of Egulac must go to war. Ookan did not want to go to war. Woozoo went on, "The Drummer has spoken. We must go."
Then Ookan became brave. He took up the drum and began to beat it. The men of Egulac came running from their homes. They were afraid. Ookan told them, "The Drummer has spoken. We must go to war."
And so the young men of Egulac went to war. Some of them went in canoes across the river. Some of them went by land. They went against the Sioux and the Cheyenne and the Arapaho. They went against the men of the Plains of Amboy. They went against the men of Ppiabo. They went against the men of Wah-ne-yage. And they went against the men of Pan-pa-ka-wun-nee.

An old sea dog of a Cree came walking along the beach and he noticed the two young men and noticed they were in trouble and he wondered what happened.  They were hunting seals but the fog was so thick they could hardly see their hands in front of their faces, let alone the seals.
The old sea dog asked the young men if he could sing a song to drive the seals closer to the shore and the young men agreed that they would try anything.  When the old dog began to sing the young men could distinctly hear the beat of the drums in the background.  The beat of the drums was driving the seals closer to the shore and soon the young men could see the seals swimming towards them.  They were able to grab two large seals and brought them back to their village where they fed themselves and their families very well.  After they had finished eating the old sea dog asked the young men if they would like to hear another song, but they declined and he left them alone.  The young men were very grateful for the old sea dog's help and they named their children after him.  His name was Waban.
Waban was a powerful spirit and his name lived on through the young men's children and their children after them.  The Cree people told many stories about Waban, the powerful spirit who helped them hunt seals.

One of the young men, Kadlek, was riding in a canoe with his dog Kana when a spirit appeared before them. The tribal people of the area lived in longhouses built on stilts alongside the river and the young men heard the sound of drums in the distance.  They shouted to the drummers that they were going to attack from the land side.  The drummers replied that they were already aware of that and that their drums were only to help guide the spirits.
The young men attacked and managed to kill a couple of seals, but then realized that the drummers were not their enemies.  The two sides negotiated and agreed that the tribal people would help the hunters in the future.  This alliance proved to be very successful and the two groups worked together to prosper.
This is an example of  how Indigenous peoples from the Pacific Northwest exchanged goods and services with one another, and how alliances were formed through the potlatch system.  The potlatch was a traditional method of celebrating special occasions and transferring wealth and property from one generation to the next.  It involved a feast, followed by gift-giving.  The more valuable the gift, the more respect it commanded.  Gifts were often given to outsiders as a sign of goodwill and to forge alliances.  The Haida, Tlingit, and Tsimshian were some of the tribes that participated in the potlatch system.

What did the young men see when they approached the seals?
The young men saw that the seals had the shapes of human beings.

The Moral of the Story
The story tells us that in order to understand something fully, we must approach it with an open mind and a willingness to learn. The young men in the story were initially confused by the sight of seals on land, but their curiosity and open-mindedness led them to discover an important truth about the creatures they were hunting.

The boys were likely using spears to hunt the seals.  Spears were the most common hunting tool used by indigenous people in the Pacific Northwest.  The boys would have to get very close to the seals in order to use their spears effectively, which is why they were hunting at night when there was no sunlight to give away their positions.  If the seals heard them coming, they would dive under the water and stay there until the threat passed.

They heard the distant sound of drums. The young men were Ogles by name, and they were hunters. They wondered where the drums were coming from, and they decided to follow the sound. They followed the sound, and it seemed to come closer and closer. Finally, they came to a small clearing, and there they saw a large circle of men, dancing and drumming. The young men were amazed, and they watched for a while as the men danced and drummed. Then, suddenly, the circle of men was surrounded by a large group of warriors from a nearby village. The young men realized that this was a gathering of the tribe, and that the drumming was a call to war. They turned and ran back to their own village, and told their people what they had seen. From that day on, the young men of Egulac were prepared for war.

The next time the drums sounded, the young men from Egulac were ready. They grabbed their weapons and ran to join the battle. The fighting was fierce, but the Egulac warriors were strong and brave. They fought with all their might, and they pushed back the enemy forces. The young men of Egulac were hailed as heroes, and they became the leaders of the tribe. From that day on, the drums were always heard in times of war.

Many years later, the old chief of the tribe lay dying. His people gathered around him, and he told them the story of the drums. He told them that the drums were a gift from the Great Spirit, and that they were meant to be used only in times of war. He told them that the younger generation must always be prepared for battle, and that they must never forget the sacrifices that their ancestors had made. And he told them that, although the drums were a powerful tool, they must always be used with honor and respect. The young men listened carefully to their chief's words, and they vowed to carry on his legacy.

They heard the distinct barking of humpback whales in the distance. One of them, Kow-Kud, lived at Tavoy and was a powerful man. He suggested to his companion, Tuck-Tuck, that they swim out to the shipwreck, Shigir, which was in the middle of the river. It was a risky move, especially for Tuck-Tuck who was a poor swimmer. A young woman from Peggys cove came by and offered them refreshment. She took them to her house and fed them, giving them venison and bread and buttered beans. After they had eaten, she laid them down on straw mats in a sunny corner of the hut and massaged their feet. Then she sang to them in a soothing voice. Lulled by the warmth of the hut, the soft touch, the sweet music, the two young men fell into a deep sleep. When they awoke it was morning and the fog had lifted. The young women smiled and said, "Now you are ready to hunt seals."
For seven days the young men remained in the hut feasting on the hospitality of the young woman. On the eighth day they set out to hunt seals and succeeded in getting as many as they needed. They returned to the hut to thank the young woman for her help. She smiled and said, "I am glad you enjoyed your stay."
The young men returned to their village, where they were welcomed as heros. They told the story of the young woman from Peggy's Cove who had helped them in their time of need. From that day on, the two young men were known as "The Two Heroes of Peggy's Cove."

The young men were Coyote and Wolf.  Coyote was blowing on his pipe, puffing away as he sat on a rock by the river's edge.  Suddenly, a seal popped its head above the water and stared at Coyote.  Coyote was startled and dropped his pipe into the water.  The seal dove and retrieved it, then swam away.  Wolf saw this and thought he would try his hand at fishing.  He took a bone and tossed it into the water.  A frog grabbed it and swallowed it whole.  Wolf pulled on the frog's legs and tail, but the frog wouldn't budge.  Coyote came over and whispered in the frog's ear, "Let go of the bone, I'll make you a deal."  The frog let go and Coyote gave it a nice, juicy grasshopper.  Then Coyote blew on his pipe and the wind came up.  The water was churned and fouled by the wind and the fog, and the young men went home empty-handed.
On their way home, Coyote and Wolf came across a pile of bones by the side of the trail.  There were hare, rabbit, fox, and wolf bones.  Coyote said, "Let's make a stew."  They built a fire and put the bones in a pot with some water.  They added some berries for flavor and soon had a delicious stew.  As they sat down to eat, the sun came up and the fog lifted.  They could see the bones in the light and realized that they were eating their own ancestors.  They felt ashamed and left the bones behind as they continued on their journey.

The young men from Egulac were Natives of the lower Fraser River country. They were out one night in early spring,  hunting seals, when a fog rose and enveloped them.  They could no longer see each other, and, because the hunting of seals was a communal activity, they returned home empty-handed. The tide was running strongly, and the current was sweeping the man named Nootka at the time into the rapids. His companion, who was named Haloetl, called out to him, "Nootka, I can't swim against this current. What shall we do?"
And Nootka replied, "Hold on to the rocks, Haloetl. I'll help you."
Then Nootka swam out to an island that was near at hand, and brought back to Haloetl a large driftwood log. 
Holding the log in front of him as a raft, he sat down on it, and told Haloetl to get on the log with him. 
With the log to help them both, the two young men were able to make their way through the rapids and out of the fog and into the open water.
Once they were clear of the dangers of the rapids, Nootka stood up on the log and struck out powerfully with his paddle, propelling the log and himself forward with great force.
"Look, Haloetl, we are now in open water. We can catch our breath and continue our hunt for seals."
Haloetl looked around him and saw that Nootka was right: the fog had lifted, and the sun was now shining down on the water, making it easy for them to see the seals basking on the rocks.
Together, the two young men continued their journey down the river, using the log as a raft to help them navigate the rapids.
And so, by working together and using the natural resources around them, Nootka and Haloetl were able to overcome the dangers of the rapids and continue their hunt for seals.

The young men were about to return home when they heard the sound of paddles in the fog. They strained their ears and listened and then heard it again. It was the sound of many paddles. They looked at each other and then set off again in the fog.
They followed the sound of the paddles and soon saw a canoe coming through the fog towards them. It was the clan canoe of the Tlingit people. The young men knew that it was dangerous to travel at night in the fog so they had come out to meet the Tlingit canoe.
The Tlingit people were trading goods and the young men exchanged some of their goods with the Tlingit people. Then the Tlingit people continued on their journey. The young men returned home safely.

The story is told in Charles E. Beckett's book, "Tales of the Tlingit".

Another interpretation of this story is that the young men were not from Egulac but from Yaxtun. In this interpretation, the young men were on a fishing trip when they heard the sound of paddles. They followed the sound and saw the Tlingit canoe in the fog. The Tlingit people welcomed them aboard and they travelled together for some time. The young men learned many things from the Tlingit people. When they had learned as much as they could, they returned to their own people.

This story has been retold many times. It has been retold in books such as "Katherine Beckett's Tlingit Tales" (1910), "Tales of the Tlingit" (1918), and "The People of the Rainforest" (1997). It has also been retold orally, in publications such as "Language and Culture Preservation through Children's Books: Revitalizing Tlingit" (2010).

The wind came up suddenly and without warning.  The two young men were caught out in the boat and could not make it to shore. They called out to the Spirit of the River for help and the Spirit of the River came to their aid. She drove the fog away and lifted the calm. The young men were able to make it to shore safely.

The story continues that the young men were full of gratitude for the help they had received and offered gifts to the Spirit of the River. The Chief's daughter, Kinmah, was the Spirit of the River and she selected the best gift, a new canoe. The young men named the canoe Ikumma, which means "heart of the river." The heart of the river is a powerful spirit being that provides for the people and keeps them safe.
The people of Egulac were very religious and believed in many spirit beings that helped them in various ways. The Spirit of the River was one of their most important deities.  When the people moved to Fort Ellice they took Ikumma with them and it became the first church in the settlement.  The people continued to use the canoe as a church and it was still there when Europeans arrived.  A European settler named Thomas Scott wrote in his journal that the natives talked about the "Holy Canoe".

The story of Ikumma, the Spirit of the River, is a story of gratitude and respect for the natural world. It is a story that reminds us of the important relationships that Indigenous peoples had with the land, the water, and the creatures that lived there. It is a story that reminds us of the wisdom that can be found in Indigenous traditions and the important lessons that we can learn from them.

The young men were wondering what to do when they heard a voice calling out in a cheerful tone: "Come, my children, and join in the dance. Let not the flame scare you. Across the water is the road to life; but here is the road to happiness."

The young men were shy and hesitated. Then one of them said, "We do not know your dance."
The old chief who was sitting nearest to them beckoned them over and said, "Your dance is our dance, my children. We have been expecting you. It is good to see you. You are welcome to join us in the dance."
So the young men went forward and joined in the dance. They ate and were merry and took their place in the circle at the fire. Then the fire-giver stood up and went across the water to his own dwelling. The young men continued to dance all night long. When the morning came they went back to their own people, singing and happy. From that time forward they loved the circular fire at the river, and it came to be their custom to build such a fire at every hunt.

They looked back and saw that the river was on fire! They had never seen such a thing before. The flames were shaking the trees on the bank of the river.
The young men were terrified and they didn't know what to do. Suddenly, they heard a voice behind them. It was the Great Spirit. He told them not to be afraid, and that he had sent the flames to light up the night sky for them.
The young men were still afraid, but the Great Spirit reassured them. He told them that he would protect them. And then he made the flames go away.
The young men got into their canoe and paddled back to the safety of their camp. They were very relieved to be back home.
The next day, they went to the place where they had seen the fire. All they found was some burnt grass and trees. They saw that the fire had not harmed the river, and they realized that the Great Spirit had protected them.

Commentary
This is a classic example of a "portal story," in which a supernatural event serves as an occasion for conveying wisdom. In this case, the story reveals that the young men of Egulac are easily frightened and lack courage, but the Chief reassures them that there is nothing to be afraid of. The story also implies that the young men are inexperienced and lack knowledge, since they do not recognize the wind as a natural phenomenon. The women are also affected by the whispering, suggesting that the event is a portent of change, perhaps a change in the social order. The twin brothers were hunting for seals near the mouth of the Niagara River, where it became foggy and calm. As they neared the Canadian shore, they heard the sound of rifles and shouts in the mist. They stumbled upon a group of Iroquois, who were also hunting seals. The Iroquois invited the young men to join them, and they spent the night hunting and sharing stories. In the morning, the young men returned to their canoe and paddled back to their village, where they told their family and friends about their adventure and the generosity of the Iroquois. From that point on, the young men and the Iroquois became friends and traded regularly. This event marked the beginning of relations between the Haudenosaunee (Iroquois) and the people of the Niagara region.

Story summary
The story is summarized as follows:

Two young men from Egulac went down to the river to hunt seals. It was foggy and calm. They heard rifle fire and shouts in the mist, and came upon a group of Iroquois who were also hunting seals. The Iroquois invited them to join, and they spent the night hunting and sharing stories. In the morning, they returned home and told their family and friends about their adventure and the generosity of the Iroquois. From that point on, they became friends and traded regularly.

Story analysis
This is a creation story, in that it explains how the relationship between the Haudenosaunee (Iroquois) and the people of the Niagara region began. It is also a coming-of-age story, as the young men in the story are probably brothers who are hunting seals to prove their maturity and ability to provide for their family and community. The story also emphasizes the importance of friendship and trust in inter-tribal relations.
