And one of the young men, whose name was Koola, called out to the other young man, whose name was Kan.

And he said: "Kan, I think I see an otter."
"Kan nothing is there," replied the other.
"Maybe it is a caribou."
"Caribou do not come down to the river."
"Then it must be an eel."
"Eels do not come out in the fog."
Upon this Koola laughed, and said: "You are nothing but a fool, Kan. You do not know anything about the ways of the universe."
And so it often happens that two young men who spend much time together in the wilderness develop a great understanding, and even a great love, for one another. But in this case, it was not to be, for just then a great wave came crashing down upon them and swept Kan away, never to be seen again.
And Koola, the survivor, was left alone, but he was not lonely, for he knew that his beloved Kan would some day return to him.
And so it was that Koola, the survivor, waited and waited for his beloved Kan, and when the time came for him to depart from this earthly plane, Kan was there beside him, and together they journeyed on to the next.

Background
The story is from the novel "The Song of Hiawatha" by Henry Wadsworth Longfellow.  The character Hiawatha does not appear in this excerpt.  The story is told by the narrator, who identifies himself as the "Wilderness Boy".  The novel was published in 1855.  The legend of the Hauchins (also spelled Houcheins) is from the Algonquian legend told by the Penobscot Nation.  The legend says that the Hauchins were the spirits of the dead who would appear to the living and either help or harm them, depending on the actions of the living while they were alive.  The Penobscot Nation is from Maine, and the Rogue River, where the story takes place, is in Oregon, so it appears that Longfellow has combined two distinct legends.

Two young men from Egulac went down to the river to hunt seals. It was a sunny day when they started, but by the time they had gotten to the river it became foggy and calm. They could hear the water lapping against the shore, and the only sound in the air was the call of a distant loon. The hunters knew that they were in for a long wait.
They sat in their canoe and smoked their pipes, watching the fog roll in across the river. After a while they heard the faint sound of drums in the distance. The drums grew louder, and soon the hunters could see the source of the sound: a group of five canoes, approaching from the west.
The hunters from Egulac greeted the others with the peaceful sign language that their people used, and the visitors from the west replied with similar gestures. Together, the two groups searched for seals all night, but they were unsuccessful. At dawn, the hunters from the west packed up their belongings and paddled away, leaving the hunters from Egulac to continue their hunt alone.
The young men from Egulac knew that they would not have much luck hunting seals by themselves, but they decided to stay by the river a little longer. As the day wore on, the fog lifted and the sun came out. The hunters could now see the rocky shoreline, and they could see that there were no seals to be found. They packed up their belongings and paddled back to their village, disappointed but determined to try again another day.

The young men were Yali and Telic. Yali was expert in calling forth the spirits of the dead, and Telic was expert in throwing the spear. They went down to the river to hunt seals because the winter had been very hard and there was no food.
Now it was foggy and calm, and the spirits of the dead were active. Yali begin to call forth the spirits of his ancestors, and they came to him. Yali told them that there was a great fog over the river, and the spirits could not cross. The spirit of his brother, Tlelo, said, "Tell them to call us over. We will help you hunt the seals."
Yali called to the spirits of his brother and cousin, and they came to help him. Together they hunted the seals, and Yali's clan had enough to eat for the winter.
Later, Yali became chief of his clan, and he told his people to always remember the time when the spirits of the dead came to help them hunt seals during a great fog.

They heard the distinct barking of seals, but couldn't see them. Suddenly, three seals appeared in the air and landed in front of the young men. The young men were amazed. The seals talked and proposed that they go to war with the people from the nearby town, in exchange for the young men teaching them how to use the weapons of the people. The young men agreed and they went to war and defeated the people from the town. Afterwards, the seals taught the young men how to hunt seals.

The young men went back to their village and told of their adventures with the seals. The people were amazed and asked them how they had accomplished such a great feat. The young men replied, "We didn't do it ourselves. It was the work of the great Spirit."
After several more adventures, the young men decided to leave their village and go to the town by the sea. While they were there, they met a young woman and one of the young men fell in love with her. He married her and they lived happily ever after.

Commentary
Ojibwe stories often involve animals and in this story, the otters are curious and active, while the young men are cautious and observant.  The calm and foggy night, with the moon coming out, is a common setting for Ojibwe stories.  The young men are hunting seals, a difficult and dangerous task, but one that is essential for their survival.  The fact that they are able to continue their journey after this encounter shows their resilience and determination.

Characters: The story features two named young men from Egulac, but the otters are the most prominent characters.  The young men are typically quiet and observant, while the otters are active and curious.

They told their hosts about the otters, but their words were laughed at. "You young men are always imagining things," they were told. The Morale
The story is often told to illustrate the value of firsthand experience over secondhand information. It also emphasizes the importance of observation in establishing truth. In scientific terminology, this story illustrates the principle of empiricism.
In Tlingit legend, the story refers to two important spiritual beings, Transformer and Keeper, who appear in many stories. In this story, Transformer is represented by the sea otters, and Keeper is represented by the young men from Egulac, who had the good fortune to encounter Transformer and learn from him.

In time the young man recovered and learned to hunt again.  He returned to his tribe and told them what had happened.  His people were shocked and saddened by his story.  His tribe could not believe that he had been alone and unprotected.  They decided that no one should hunt alone and that they would hunt in groups from then on.  The young man's injury became a badge of honour and a reminder of the importance of community.

Suddenly they heard a strange sound. One of them said, "That sounds like the heartbeat of the earth." They followed the sound and found that it was coming from a large stone.  When they approached the stone it spoke to them. It told them that it was an ancient stone put there by the First Man. It had been there to keep the water pure for the salmon to swim upstream to their spawning grounds.  The stone had been there for thousands of years, and it was now passing its power on to a new stone.
The two young men were very impressed and went back to their people to tell them of their adventure.  Their people told them that they were very lucky to have had such an experience.  The stone would now become a landmark for the tribe, and the young men were named by the tribe as the keepers of the stone.  Every year after that, on the anniversary of their adventure, the young men would take their sons and daughters to the river to teach them about the stone and the importance of keeping the water pure for the salmon.
Many years went by and the young men grew old and had children of their own.  One day, a great flood came and washed the stone away.  The keepers of the stone were very sad but knew that the stone would appear again some day.  They continued to tell the story of the stone to their descendants for many, many generations.
Finally, one day, a young boy named Taku was playing by the river and he found the stone.  He brought it back to his people and they were very excited to have the stone back again.  They put it in a special place in the longhouse and treated it with great respect.
From that day on, every time the people saw the stone, they were reminded of the adventure of the two young men and the importance of keeping the water pure for the salmon.

The two young men were hunting seals when suddenly it became foggy and calm. They decided to stop hunting and to make their way back to the village. As they were walking along the shore, they heard a strange noise behind them. They turned around and saw a giant sea monster emerging from the water. It let out a loud hiss and charged towards them. The young men ran as fast as they could, but the monster grabbed one of them and dragged him back into the water. The other young man managed to escape and ran back to the village to warn the other members of his tribe. They all went down to the shore to hunt the sea monster. When they arrived, they saw that it was a giant octopus. They shot it with their bows and spears, but it didn't seem to harm it. One of the young men came up with the idea to use fire against the octopus. They gathered some wood and created a fire on the shore. The octopus came out of the water and wrapped its tentacles around the fire. The young men threw their spears and arrows at the octopus, but it continued to wrap itself around the fire. The young men realized that the fire was not hurting the octopus, so they ran away as fast as they could. The octopus went back into the water and disappeared. The young men returned to the village and told the story of the sea monster and how they had tried to destroy it but failed. From that day on, the young men became known as Takucha (brave) and Wakuta (clever). Takucha was the name given to the young man who had escaped the octopus, and Wakuta was the name given to the young man who had come up with the plan to use fire against the octopus. The story of Takucha and Wakuta was passed down from generation to generation, and became a legend among the Egulac people.

The young men were Ookana and Tanoo. Ookana was an expert hunter, and Tanoo was a powerful conjurer. They were on the lookout for a large herd of seals that was reported to be in the area.
As they continued their hunt, the fog became thicker and the men could no longer see each other. Ookana chased after a seal, but in the confusion, he lost his way back to the village. Tanoo, meanwhile, used his powers to conjure up a large eagle to help him locate his friend.
The eagle soared through the fog, searching for Ookana. Soon it spotted him, trapped between the shore and a narrow inlet. The eagle led Tanoo to his friend, and the two men emerged unharmed. However, they could not find the herd of seals.
As they paddled back to their village, the fog lifted and the sun rose. Ookana and Tanoo saw that the herd of seals had been there all along, only a short distance from the shore. They cursed their bad luck, but then laughed at their mistake. After all, who would expect seals to be so close to the surface?
The men returned to their village, empty-handed but happy to be alive. They knew that their friendship and the power of teamwork had saved them from certain death in the fog. From that day on, Ookana focused on hunting, while Tanoo used his powers to help guide their journeys. Together, they became an unbeatable team, respected throughout the land for their courage and determination.

Ojas and Wassah survived, and told the story to their own people, who voted to move to a new village site further upriver, where they could see the approaching Americans.

Suddenly a huge wild beast came down to the river's edge and stood facing them, shaking the ground with each of its steps. It had enormous teeth and eyes that glowed in the fog. The young men could not move or speak, they could only stare at the beast. The beast then lay down on the ground and went to sleep. The old people in the village said that the beast was M’Seliuhk, the killer whale, who had come in from the ocean to hunt them. Another version says that it was the spirit of the river, always there, but usually hidden from the senses of the humans. In time, the young men learned to live with M’Seliuhk, and even learned to communicate with it. They built a shrine to it on the banks of the river, and made offerings to it regularly. Then, and only then, were they able to hunt seals there again.

Raven, in Nagano tradition, is a trickster figure who lives by the river. He is often mischievous and causes problems for humans, but he is also helpful and plays an important role in the creation story.

Story:
According to the story, in the beginning there was only water, the primal ocean. The Creator, Tsona, decided to create the earth and the people. Tsona spoke to Raven, the trickster, and commanded him to create the land. Raven flew up to the heavens and threw down the mountains and the islands. 
After the land was created, Tsona spoke to Raven again and commanded him to create the rivers. Raven flew up to the heavens once more and brought down the rivers. 
When the people were created, Raven became their teacher and guide. He taught them how to make tools and weapons. He showed them how to hunt and fish. He even taught them how to tell stories. 
But Raven was mischievous. He played many tricks on the people. He would often take the form of a raven and fly overhead, mocking them. But the people learned to ignore him and continued their lives.

The water smelled good and the young men felt that something was happening. 
At this point one of the young men, Pau-Pau-Kai, stood up in the canoe and shouted out "By the teeth of the Raven, the Salmon will come."  Suddenly the water began to boil and twist and then a salmon jumped into the air and landed into their canoe.  The young men were amazed and thrilled by this turn of events.  They continued to shake their canoe and chant "By the teeth of the Raven, the Salmon will come."  Soon more and more salmon jumped into their canoe until it was full.  The young men were now very happy and grateful for the gift of the Salmon.
Pau-Pau-Kai reached out his hand and touched the salmon and said "I give you back to the water, to the water, to the water."  The salmon then swam away.  The young men ate some of the salmon and saved some for the journey back to their village.  They sang and danced on the shoreline thanking the Raven for the gift of the Salmon.
The other young man, Tashi-Tashi, built a fire on the beach and cooked the rest of the salmon.  While they were eating, Tashi-Tashi reached into the ashes of the fire and pulled out a bonesoup.  He blew on it and suddenly it came to life and began to dance around the fire.  The young men were afraid and hurried to put the bonesoup back into the fire.  They continued to eat their meal while watching the fire jump and crackle.
Suddenly Pau-Pau-Kai stood up and shouted out "By the teeth of the Raven, the Fire will come."  The fire grew larger and brighter and the young men were consumed by the flames.  They died quickly and their spirits joined the spirits of their ancestors

The two young men were exploring a possible new trading route when they were caught in a storm on the river and lost their way. They put into an island and made camp there. 
Although they had brought their weapons with them, they did not have any food. They looked at their maps and saw that they were near an Ojibway village and decided tomake their way there. They began to hunt and fish along the shore but failed to get anything. Soon they became so famished that they began to eat the bark of trees to survive.
When they finally reached the village, the people there were very friendly to them and showed them great hospitality. The young men bartered some furs for food and thus managed to survive. When it was time to leave, the villagers gave them a send-off and warned them about the fog that frequently made navigation on the river difficult.
The two young men returned home and told their tale to the other members of their band. From that time on, whenever any of them went down to the river to hunt, they sent a canoe ahead to scout the route and to keep a lookout for fog.

Background
The story is told by Tecumseth in Walter Scott's Red Book of Canada (1897), based on legends told to him by the Ojibway people.

The tide was running heavily and the current was extremely strong.  The two young men were hunting for seals on the far side of a sand bar when they were pulled apart by the current.  One of them was a strong swimmer and a good swimmer at that, but the other one was a very average swimmer at best.  The good swimmer managed to get back to the sand bar and struggled back to the village, exhausted but alive.  The other young man was not so lucky.  He was swept out of the river by the current and soon lost sight of the village.  He was tired but still afloat when he was picked up by a passing fishing boat.  The fishermen pulled him out of the water and revived him with some tea and then dropped him off at the village.  When the young man from Egulac got back to the village, he was greeted with celebration because everyone thought he was dead.  His sister-in-law even prepared a meal for him, not knowing that it was him who had returned.  When he went to bed that night, he was exhausted but happy to be alive.
As the young man lay there in the dark, he began to think about the events that had transpired that night and he began to wonder.  He wondered if the fog and the current had been sent to test him, to see if he was worthy of continuing his life.  He wondered if the village would be there when he returned and if his loved ones would still be there.  He began to realize that life was very fragile and that it could be easily snuffed out at any moment.  He also realized that he had been given a second chance and that he needed to make the most of it.  So, he made a vow that he would live his life to the fullest and that he would not squander the second chance that he had been given.
From that night on, the young man from Egulac lived his life to the fullest.

A young woman from Kispiox arrived at the camping ground. The two young men welcomed her and offered her some food. She accepted their offer and sat down with them. They began to talk about their families and their tribes. The young woman was impressed by their hospitality and later on she married one of the young men. She moved in with his family and learned their ways. Her children were taught the ways of the Kwakwaka'wak people.
After many years of living with the Kwakwaka'wak people, the young woman became a prominent member of the tribe. She was well known for her beautiful singing voice and was often asked to perform at important ceremonies. Her songs were passed down through the generations and are still sung today.

In the end
The tale of the young woman who married into the Kwakwaka'wak people illustrates the importance of hospitality and cooperation among different tribes. It also highlights the rich cultural heritage of the First Nations people of Canada.

Eventually, he asked her if she would marry him, and she said that she would be happy to. 
So, Cedric and Laureline were married, and the young men of Egulac were very happy for their friend. 
They continued to hunt seals and tell stories by the fire, now with the knowledge that love and happiness could come from the most unexpected of places.

The young men were fishing for eels in a creek that ran into the river when they heard the distinct barking of hidden wolves. The wolves were hiding their eyes, waiting for the young men to step into the open.
One young man named Tcho-chin was an expert tracker and he perceived that there were five wolves.
Tcho-chin said to his companion, "We are in great danger! The wolves are waiting for us to step into the open. We must wait until light before we try to return home."

Tcho-chin said, "I count five eyes. There are five wolves. We can't outrun them. We can't fight them. We must play dead."
The young men lay down on the ground and played dead. The wolves came closer and began to sniff at them. Tcho-chin and his companion played dead until the wolves lost interest and went away.
When the young men were sure that the wolves had left, they got up and ran home as fast as they could. They told their people what had happened and their people decided that they must move to a new camp.
The young men's people built a new camp by the sunflower meadow. The wolves came to the new camp and the young men played dead again. The wolves left after a while and the young men's people built a wall of bones around the camp for protection.
From that time on, the young men's people were safe from the wolves.
The young men were now elders and they told this story to the young people. The young people listened to the elders and learned from their experiences.

One night two young men from Egulac went down to the river to hunt seals and while they were there it became foggy and calm. What happened (in detail)?

The young men were exploring a large island that was covered with thick brush when they heard the screaming of many women. 
They pushed their way through the brush and emerged onto a beach where they saw a strange sight. A large circle had been drawn in the sand by many hands, and within it were many women, all naked and dancing wildly. The younger of the two men was frightened, but the other told him that these were the Tlashtsi women, who were famous for being beautiful and powerful in the old days. His friend advised him to be respectful and watch the women dance for a while. As they continued to watch, the younger man began to feel a deep connection to the women and a great sadness. He knew that these women were sad, not happy, and that they were waiting for something or someone. Suddenly, one of the women spoke up and asked if the young men were from Egulac. The young men replied that they were. The woman then asked if they knew a girl named Kosana. The younger man said that he did. The woman told him that Kosana was dead, that she had died waiting for her lover to return from the war. The younger man was shocked and saddened by this news. The women then continued to dance wildly around the young men, singing a sad song. The younger man felt that he was being drawn into their dance, and he closed his eyes and began to dance with them. When he opened his eyes, he saw that the women had vanished, leaving only footprints in the sand. The young men then returned to their village, where the old people told them that the Tlashtsi women were powerful and that the young men had been lucky to see them. From that day on, the young men were respected by the people of their village.

One of the young men suggested that they return home, but the other suggested that they wait and see what will happen. They decided to wait and were rewarded by seeing a great big stag crawl out of the fog onto the shore. The young men proceeded to hunt the stag and killed it. They took its horns and left the body there in the fog. When they returned home, they were amazed to find that the fog had turned into a great feast. The young men were transformed into beings with horns and hooves, and their mother, who was a cannibal, was very pleased with their transformation and told them that they could now hunt her enemies. The young men went out to hunt and met a being who told them that he was the sun. They asked him if he would go slow for them and he agreed. They proceeded to hunt and their minds became one with the trees and the rivers and the winds. Finally, they came upon a being who was too strong for them and they died. Their bodies were transformed into two great trees which stood beside the river. Their names were Otter and Beaver.

Commentary
This story relates the transformation of two young men from Egulac into otter and beaver, important creatures in the First Nations' natural world. The story also illustrates the importance of transformation in First Nations' belief systems. Transformation is a common motif in Native American stories. In this story, transformation occurs through hunting and eating the flesh of a sacred creature. Transformation can also be seen in the sun's transformation from a being to an event.

Story origins
This story was told by a First Nations' storyteller to Tantalis Quesnell, who recorded it in his book, Native Tales of the Northwest Coast. Quesnell did not indicate which nation the storyteller belonged to.

Variations
This story has several variations. One variation is found in the book, Traditional Tales of the Northwest

The river was calm and smooth, and the fog was so thick they could hardly see their hands in front of their faces. Suddenly they heard a strange sound. It was like the sound of a man crying. They listened carefully and understood that it was not a man but the river itself that was crying.
They searched around and saw that the source of the crying was a dead body of a Cree woman who had been thrown into the river by her husband. Her husband was a white man and when he threw her body into the river, he wept.
The two young men decided to search for her family and let them know what had happened. They went to the village of the Cree woman's family and told them what had happened. The family was very angry and went to the village of the white man. They told him what had happened and demanded that he give them the body of their sister so that they could bury her properly.
The white man was very sorry for what he had done and he gave them the body. He also gave them a great deal of money to help them through this difficult time. The Cree family was comforted by the fact that their sister would be properly buried and that they would be able to put their grief behind them.
The young men returned to their own village and told their friends what had happened. From that day on, the young men were known as Gloomy Bob and Cold Cream. Gloomy Bob was always sad and melted the hearts of all who met him. Cold Cream was always funny and made everyone laugh.
Together, the two young men brought joy and comfort to their people during a time of grief. And the river, which had once cried, was now calm and smooth once more.

And one of them said to the other: "We are silly to sit here and do nothing; let us carry out our plan and catch some seals."
And the other said: "But how can we catch seals in this fog and calm?"
And the first said: "The fog and calm will help us; the seals will come to the shore to breathe and we will catch them."
And so they proceeded to catch many seals and made a good catch that night.
And the moon mirrored in the quiet water, on the surface they did not disturb.
And the quiet was interrupted only by the sounds of their harpoons driving into the seals.
And the cliffs echoed with the crashing of the waves against the shore.
And the stillness was broken only by the gentle lapping of the water against the boat.
And the two young men worked in unison, one driving the boat, the other throwing the harpoons.
And the fog lifted a little and the stars came out and the moon took its place.
And the two young men headed back to their camp, feeling proud and happy with their catch of the night.
And the night was quiet again, except for the sound of the fire crackling as the men cooked their catch.
And they told their story to the other clansmen, who all agreed it was a good hunt.
And the young men went to sleep, satisfied and content with their lives.
And the fog and calm returned, enveloping the water and the land, as if quietly acknowledging the hunt that had taken place.
And the two young men woke up early the next morning, ready to hunt again.

They heard the distinct screaming of an owl, and then they heard it again and then they saw it. It was a "mighty" great horned owl, as big as a man, with a cabin built on its back.
The young men were amazed and overwhelmed by the sight of the owl, and the owl spoke to them in a mystical way, saying: "I will not harm you, I will protect you. You are powerful like me."
After that night, the young men from Egulac took the names Taro and Tani. They became the protectors of their tribe, and no one dared to harm them. They had many adventures, and their people told many stories about them, their adventures, and their protection.
Taro and Tani became the symbols of courage and power among the young men of Egulac, and their legacy has lasted until today.

The story reminds us that Indigenous peoples have always traded and interacted with one another. One of the young men, Ahem, was expert in the art of divination and while his companion was hunting seals he sat down by the fire to divine about their future. 
Ahem had a pipe heused for drawing divinations on the water surface. He started to pipe and soon the water surface became cloudy and then cleared to show a scene.
The scene that appeared showed a huge monster lying on its side with its head facing the two young men. The monster had great teeth, like the teeth of a grizly bear and its eyes were as large as the full moon.
Ahem told his companion that this was no ordinary monster but was a being from the other world, a being that was trying to communicate with them. He told his companion that they should not be afraid but should approach the being slowly and respectfully and try to communicate with it.
His companion agreed and they both swam towards the being. When they were close they could see that the being was not hostile and had the form of a large seal with strange growths on its back.
The young men approached the being and tried to touch it and the being responded by lifting its head and roaring loudly. The young men were frightened and swam away.
For several days the young men did not hunt and instead sat on the shore watching the monster in the water. They tried again to approach the monster and this time they were not frightened. They touched the growths on the monster's back and the being responded by lifting its head and blowing bubbles of air through its nostrils.
The young men interpreted this as a friendly sign and they swam around the being, touching it and playing with it. 
After several days of this, the being disappeared and the young men returned to their people. They told the story of the being from the other world and how it had communicated with them.
From that day on, the young men were respected among their people for having had a supernatural experience.

While the women were gone, the men talked about how they had thought the women were laughing at them, but now saw that they were being invited to join them. The men felt happy, and the women felt happy too, especially when the men joined in their laughter. After the women had returned with the dry cloths, they all sat down together and began to eat and share stories. As the sun came up, the men and women stood up and went their separate ways, but with a feeling of happiness and friendship between them.

The wind came up sudden and strong enough to capsize their canoes, but they managed to right them before any damage was done. They continued to hunt and were successful in catching six seals.
On their way back home, they entered a narrow channel between two islands, where the wind blew even stronger than before. The young men stared in terror as their canoes were tossed about by the wind and waves. They were soon driven back to where they had caught the seals, and there they were swallowed up by the earth as the land rose up to block their escape.
The young men had been Bentsho and Tatoosh, and their story became known as the "Tale of Bentsho and Tatoosh." It was told and retold many times, becoming a classic of native storytelling. In its various versions, the two young men were often said to have been brothers, and the event took place not at Amgiverk, but at Kakevik, near Kake. In still other tellings, the two young men were not hunters at all, but rather tricksters who played with the elements of fire and water, and who, in the version told by William Henry Smith in 1907, were transformed into the sun and moon.

The young men were about to give up and make their way back to the village when they heard the sound of a giant's drum. Following the sound, they came upon a great circular pit, the drumming was coming from inside. There they saw a giantess, Naaxiide, who was pregnant. She was sitting by a fire making drums. The young men were amazed and watched her from a distance. Suddenly she rose and went to the water's edge and began to wash her hands in the water. The young men saw that her hands were marked with X's.
The young men went to the village and told the people about what they had seen. The elders said that Naaxiide was the Spirit of the River and the X's on her hands were symbols of the Xias, the river spirits. The young men were told that they would become great hunters if they marked their own hands with X's.
Many days passed and the two young men became great hunters. They killed many caribou and cooked them over the fire. One day while they were eating, a raven perched on a nearby tree. The young men looked at the raven and thought that it was Naaxiide's spirit. They offered the raven some caribou meat, but the raven shook its head.
The young men were puzzled by this, but soon understood the raven's purpose. It was Naaxiide's spirit, but it could only accept offerings of fish, not caribou. From that day on, the young men always offered Naaxiide fish when they passed by the spot where they had seen her.
Many years later, the young men grew old and told their story to their grandchildren. The grandchildren were amazed by the story and listened to it many times. Even today, the story of the two young men and the giantess Naaxiide is told to the children of the Egulac people.

Suddenly they heard the noise of a great water wheel crashing through the mist toward them. They saw a shadowy figure bailing out of the wheel just before it passed over them. The men felt the water wheel brush against their legs as it turned overhead. They looked at each other and then shouted to the owner of the wheel to come out from hiding and reveal himself.
They heard a voicesaying there was no cause for alarm, that the owner of the wheel was merely an Englishman named Dunsmore. He emerged from his hiding place and explained that he was building a sawmill at the side of the river and that the wheel was merely a pulley to aid in the operation of the mill. The men were relieved to learn that the wheel was not a monster sent to kill them. They helped Dunsmore finish the construction of the mill and then returned to their camp.
As they sat by the fire, one of the men remarked that it was a good thing they had gone down to the river to hunt seals, otherwise they would never have met Dunsmore and helped him build the mill. The other man agreed and they both laughed at their good fortune.

The moral of the story is that sometimes things that seem scary or dangerous at first can turn out to be useful or beneficial in the end.

While hunting in the fog, one young man stumbled upon a mysterious flower with a bright light in its center. As he approached the flower, the light grew brighter and the air around him became filled with the sweet scent of the flower.

Just then, a voice came through the fog, "You have found the Flower of Legend, the Starflower. It is said that if you eat the starflower, you will gain the power of the night."

The young man hesitated for a moment, then reached out and plucked the starflower from the ground. As he took the first bite, the fog lifted and the night was illuminated by the light of the starflower. He soon became the talk of the village, and all wondered where he had found the starflower.

The young man told no one of the events that had transpired that night, for he knew that the flower was a gift from the spirits of the night, and he wished to keep it that way. But every night, the village was filled with the sweet scent of the starflower, and the young man was the only one who knew the source of the fragrance.

One night, a young woman from a neighboring village came to visit, and the young man showed her the starflower. As they stood there in the night, the young woman reached out and plucked the starflower from the ground.

As she took the first bite, the young man said, "Be careful, it is a powerful flower. It is said that if you eat the starflower, you will gain the power of the night."

The young woman laughed, "I have heard the stories, but I never believed they were true."

But as she finished the last bite of the starflower, the night sky was filled with stars, and she was filled with a power she had never felt before. She could hear the birds singing, and the trees whispered secrets in her ear.

The wind came up suddenly and without warning. It blew through the hills and turned the forests into a turbulent sea. The young men were swept away by the force of the wind. The Chilchoots said that the wind came down from the mountain tops and it was known as the 'Northern Wind'. The young men who went to hunt seals were never heard of again. Their families waited and waited for them to return but they never did. Their tragedy became a legend and a warning to other young men who went to hunt seals. It was said that the Northern Wind was a malevolent spirit, a Wind Monster, that could blow away boats, sweep away villages, and blow away people.

Suddenly they heard a strange sound. It was like the sound of people walking upstairs. They looked at each other and then shook their heads. "It must be the spirits of the dead," one of them said. "Let us go home quickly." They started to leave but the sound followed them. It was a strange sound, not like the sound of people walking, but like the sound of people swimming. They stopped for a moment and looked at each other. "Let us go back and see what it is," said the other.
They went back to the river and followed the sound. It was coming from a place where the water was shallow and bubbled up to the surface. They watched for a moment and then went home, shaken by the strange experience.

What do you know about the fossil record of fish in the region where the Egulac people lived?
The answer is: The fossil record of fish in the region where the Egulac people lived is sparse, but there are a few sites in southern Alberta that provide information on the presence of fish in the region during the Pleistocene epoch. One site in particular, the Oldman Lake site, has yielded remains of at least six different species of fish. They headed toward the light and found that it came from a canoe, which was capsized over a reef.  They managed to right the canoe and climb in. And the young man who had wanted to leave said: "Maybe we should wait by the river more often."

And so, it is told, that the Egulac people learned to balance their desires with the desires of their community, and their village prospered.

Story from "Blackfeet Legends" by Frances Jane McDade
Once upon a time, long, long ago, the Blackfoot people lived in the place where the Bellegarde River enters the Milk River.  Two young men from Egulac, Tawah and Nanaskin, were sitting by the fire one night, smoking their pipes, when they heard a strange sound.  It was far away, but they could tell that it was the sound of drums.
"Let us go and investigate," said Tawah to Nanaskin.  "Perhaps it is a medicine dance, or maybe a war dance.  We must find out."
So the two young men put on their robes and moccasins and headed for the place where the drums were coming from.  They followed the sound until they came to a clearing by the side of the Bellegarde River.  There they saw a canoe approaching through the fog.  In the bow of the canoe was their friend Tatoosh, who had become a chief, and in the stern was his wife, Bear's Daughter, paddling with all her might.  Behind them were several other canoes, also loaded with passengers.
"Greetings, O Great Chief Tatoosh," called Tawah, as the canoe drew close to the bank.  "We are your servants and we welcome you home."
"How good it is to see you, my friends," said Tatoosh, as he stepped out of the canoe

The young men were afraid to go home because it was haunted, so they lay down on the shore to wait for daybreak. 
All of a sudden they heard a strange noise and looked up to see a great big rush of water coming toward them. They barely had time to jump up and grab hold of some nearby trees before the water swept them away.
When they were pulled out of the water by the tree limbs, they saw that the rush of water had been caused by the Great Flood. 
They realized that the Earth was changing and that they had to adapt or be swept away. 
From that day on, the two young men became the first proprieters of what is now known as the Muskrat Stick Nation.

The young men were about to call it a night and head back to their village when they heard the sound of a young woman singing. 
They followed the sound and came across a beautiful young woman singing to her baby on the bank of the river. 
The young men were enchanted by the woman's beauty and began to approach her. 
The woman turned out to be Kiu Kia, the spirit of the river and she invited the young men to approach her. 
She told them that she was once a human woman who had been transformed into a spirit by the great chief Tsa-ko-ha-ha. 
She told them that if they loved the river and its creatures they could become her protectors and live with her forever. 
The young men agreed and Kiu Kia transformed them into otters, giving them the ability to breathe underwater and live in the river. 
From that day forward the young men (now otters) lived in the river and became its protectors, guided by Kiu Kia, the river spirit.

It was a bear! The two young men were scared but the one named Gedney grabbed his spear and ran towards the bear while the other ran in the opposite direction. Gedney missed the bear with his spear but the creature swung its paw towards him, hitting him on the head and knocking him unconscious.

The other young man, who was named Lokedon, saw that his friend was in trouble and so came to his aid. With great difficulty he pulled Gedney to safety behind a large rock. Lokedon took out his own spear and crept forward to attack the bear, but the bear turned towards him and charged. Lokedon threw his spear but it got stuck in the bear's paw. The bear roared in pain and anger, and then turned towards Lokedon. But just then Gedney came to his friend's aid and together the two young men killed the bear.
They collected their spears and then dragged the bear's body back to their village, where they were honoured for their bravery. From that day on the young men were known as Gedney and Lokedon, the Bear Killers.

The Moral of the Story
In this story, the young men are successful in killing the bear because they work together using their individual strengths. Gedney is strong and brave, and Lokedon is clever and quick-thinking. By combining their abilities, they are able to outwit the bear and emerge victorious. The story also shows that bear hunting is a dangerous and risky business, as the young men nearly become bear food themselves!

"I do not know that, father," the younger replied.
Then the elder spoke once more, "Do you not know that in foggy weather the visibility is more limited?"
"I do not know that, father," the younger answered again.
The elder then spoke for the third time, "Do you not know that those who hunt seals must first make theirselves like unto the seals?"
The younger man thought a moment and then replied, "I know that, father.  If I am not like the seal, I will never catch one."
The elder smiled and said, "That is true.  Now let us go home."
As they walked away from the river, the younger man asked, "Father, if I behave like a seal and wait in the water for the fish, will I then catch the fish?"
The elder laughed and said, "My son, the analogy must not be pressed too far.  Seals do not catch fish.  They feed on invertebrates on the bottom.  Now let us go home."

The river glowed with a bluish light, and on the shore there were great bright spots, as if the rocks were on fire.  The young men were puzzled by this, but continued their search for seals, calling out in the fog.
Suddenly they heard a strange sound behind them, and turning around, saw a great light approaching.  It was a strange canoe, dressed in the bones and skins of animals, with a skeleton stern and a headless prow.  It came closer and closer, until its shadow fell on the young men, who were then trapped in the canoe, which rushed them toward a great rapids.
The young men prayed to the Great Spirit, and then threw themselves into the water, just as the canoe struck the rocks and was dashed to pieces.  They swam to the shore, chilled and shaken, but otherwise unharmed, and then made their way home, where they reported what had happened to the other people of Egulac.
From that day on, the young men were known as the Tlech-gwa-de-nee-a-bu-la-tse ("Men of the Great Canoe").  They became the leaders of the tribe, and guided the people through many crises and difficulties.  Whenever the tribe was threatened, the Men of the Great Canoe would vanish, and then reappear in some distant place, where they would use their magical powers to help the tribe survive.

The young men were about to return home when they heard the sound of a cry come out of the fog. One of the young men said, "That is the cry of a wild pig."
"It is not," said the other young man. "I know that sound, it is the cry of a human baby."
And sure enough, through the fog they saw the outline of a canoe with a mother and her baby paddling toward the shore.

The young men were about to return home, but decided to wait for the sun to rise before they left the river. While they were waiting, they heard strange noises near their canoes. They drew their bows and arrows, ready to defend themselves, when they saw a raccoon. They watched the raccoon for a while, and then it picked up an apple and ate it. The young men were amazed that a raccoon could behave like a human.
Just then, a bullet fired by an unseen hand went through the air and hit the raccoon on its paw. The raccoon yelled in pain and anger, and the young men saw that there was a group of people on the other side of the river, prepared to defend their territory.
The young men realized that they were in the middle of a war between two tribes, and that they had accidentally stumbled into the middle of it. They rapidly made their way back to their own territory, where they found their own people gathered to defend against the other tribe. The young men told their fellow tribesmen about the gun, and everyone decided to build a wall to protect against future attacks. The wall worked, and the young men grew up to become great leaders of their people.
Every year after that, the two tribes would meet at the fork in the river to discuss peace and to trade goods. The young men who had accidentally started a war became the greatest of friends, and their friendship became the foundation for peace between their peoples.

They approached her again and asked her to become their sister and live with them in peace and the woman agreed. The sleigh is used to transport the potato harvest from the fields to the long houses for storage and preparation.  The young man hunting seals is a reference to the importance of fishing and hunting in the Mohawk economy and culture. Tikitu is a figure in the oral tradition of the Tlingit people. The story is retold in many variations. In some tellings, Tikitu is a man who becomes an owl, in others, he is an owl who becomes a man. In still others, he is an old man who tells stories by the fire. In all tellings, he is a trickster figure who can change shape and is mischievous. Tikitu is sometimes said to be the creator of the world, or at least, of the Raven moiety (clan) of the Tlingit people. In some stories, Tikitu appears as a spirit that helps hunters be successful. In others, he is a spirit of the dead who can be appeased with offerings of food and gifts.

The water appeared smooth and still, like a mirror. Then the young men heard strange noises. At first they thought that it was just the fog horn from one of the ships, but soon the noises grew louder and closer. Then, to their horror, they realized that it was not fog, but smoke. A steamboat was heading straight for them. The young men jumped into their canoe and paddled frantically to get out of the way, but it was no use. They felt a terrible jolt as the boat struck them. Then everything went black. When the young men came to, they found that they were trapped inside the overturned canoe, and the current was pulling them straight into the steamboat's propeller. They struggled to get free, but it was no use. Then a voice called out from the steamboat, "Are you all right?" It was the captain. He had seen the accident and was coming to help. The young men were pulled aboard the steamboat, and they watched in amazement as the captain turned the boat around and headed back to the village. The captain was hailed as a hero, and the young men were hailed as lucky. But wherever they went, they were reminded of the foggy, still night on the river when the steamboat came hunting for them.

The Moral of the story is: Be careful what you wish for, it might just come true. In this story the young men were hunting seals, when suddenly a steamboat comes hunting for them.
This story can be related to today's topic of climate change and global warming. We have been hunting for solutions to these problems for a long time, and now it seems that nature is hunting us back with increasingly frequent and severe weather events. The moral of the story remains the same: Be careful what you wish for, it might just come true.

The text seems to be written in the style of a riddle, with the answer being "it is foggy and calm on the river." The correct answer is:
One night two young men from Egulac went down to the river
To hunt seals, by the light of the moon so bright,
When suddenly the weather changed, and the fog rolled in,
Calm and still, nothing moved, not a leaf or a speck of dust,
The young men were swallowed up by the foggy night.

Answer:
The river is foggy and calm.

Creek, not river: The correct answer is:
The creek is foggy and still.

Explanation:
The word "river" in the riddle has been misunderstood by many people, including the singer of the first verse of the song "The Fisherman of Kapalanga" by Tom Lea. The word is not capitalized, and the correct answer is "creek." The riddle is often told as: "Two young men from the village of Egulac went down to the [creek] to hunt seals one night, by the light of the moon so bright. Suddenly the weather changed, and the fog rolled in, calm and still, nothing moved, not a leaf or a speck of dust. The young men were swallowed up by the foggy night."

This riddle is told by Tom Lea in his book "In Search of the Bark Canoe" (1978). It is also sung as the first verse of his song "The Fisherman of Kapalanga." The riddle is accompanied by the melody of the English folk song "The Salt Marshes of the Mermaid" (Child Ballad 18). The young men were exploring a hidden valley by the river when they heard strange noises. They rushed to their canoes and paddled to the middle of the river, where they saw a strange sight: the water was boiling, and great jets of steam were coming from the riverbanks. The young men were very frightened, but then they saw that there was a volcano in the valley behind them. They had not realized that there was a volcano near their village. They watched in awe as the lava flowed into the river, turning it into a bubbling, frothing mass. Suddenly, a great explosion shook the valley, and the young men were thrown to the ground. When they raised their heads, they saw that the volcano had collapsed into the river, blocking it.
They realized that the volcano was not active, but had gone dormant long ago. 
The young men then returned to their village, where they told their story to the other clans. Their people were very impressed by their adventure, and their boldness in exploring the hidden valley. From that day on, the young men were known as the "Hunters of the Dormant Volcano."

== Influences == 
This story is influenced by the tales of the Tlingit people. In particular, it draws on the legend of the "Frog Woman of Taku", who was said to live in a river near a volcano. 
The story also resembles the legend of the Huangdi, the Yellow Emperor, who discovered fire after investigating strange events in the forest. 
The volcano in this story is likely modeled on Mount Edgecumbe, which is both visible from Kake and dormant.

A light wind sprang up from the mouth of the Kootenay River, blowing towards the west, and blowing the mist and fog towards the Canadian side of the border. The two young men were blowing their harpoons towards the mist and fog, believing that there were seals there, when suddenly they were grabbed by two hands from behind. They were pulled back to the American side of the border, where they were turned into frogs.

Commentary
This tale is told by Orion Huntinghorse in his book "Traditional Tales of the Kootenay Region". It is a retelling of a tale told by Tkokit, as reported by Frances Beaudoin in "American Folk-Lore". The basic story is found in many cultures, including the European tale "The Frog Prince", and the African tale "Why the Tortoise has a Hard Shell". In each telling, two young men (or brothers) are transformed into frogs (or another form) as punishment for some transgression, and must live their lives in this form, often with the possibility of future transformation back to human form. In the European and African tales, the cause of the transformation is a witch or god, while in the Native American versions, it is often a trickster figure like Coyote or Raven. In each case, the transformation is brought about by the force of music or dance.

One of the young men, K'anjii, was expert in the art of divination and while his companion was hunting seals he sat down to divinate. After a long time K'anjii called out to his companion that they should return to the village, for he had divined that a great calamity was going to befall them. They returned to the village just in time to find it burned to the ground. A great disaster had befallen them, not a calamity as K'anjii had divined, but a great disaster nonetheless.
So what happened (in detail)?
The young men from Egulac had been hunting seals one night, but returned to find their village destroyed. How did they respond to this disaster?
A great disaster had indeed befallen them. The wind had shifted and the village was destroyed by fire. While K'anjii's divination had not prepared him and his companion for this disaster, it had given him the foresight to save them. They were now on their own, without food, shelter or warm clothing. They could see the fire across the sea, but in the fog they could not tell if it was still burning. They had to act quickly if they were to survive.
They had gone down to the river to hunt seals, but now the hunting season was over. The young men decided that they would have to leave their village and travel to another place. They could see the fire across the sea, and hoped that it was still burning and that they could find food and warmth there. They decided to head in that direction.
As they travelled, they came across other people who had been driven from their own villages by the fires. They joined these people and together they made their way to the place where the fires were burning most strongly. When they arrived, they found that the fires were going out and that the people were leaving. K'anjii and his companion quickly joined in the work of extinguishing the fires

The young men were about to head home, but then they saw a light on the other side of the river. They thought it might be a fire, so they headed toward it. But as they got closer, they realized it was not a fire, but a boat with people in it. The young men called out to the boat, and the people in the boat said they were going to rescue the young men, because the fog was so thick the young men could not find their way home.
So the young men got in the boat, and the people in the boat took them home. But when they got there, one of the young men said, "We must tell our people about the light on the other side of the river."
So the young men went to their people, and they told them about the light on the other side of the river. And the people said, "That is not a light, that is our relatives from the other side coming to visit us."
And from that day on, every time the fog was thick and calm on the river, the young men from Egulac would go to the other side to hunt seals and visit their relatives.

One of the young men suggested that it was better to go back to the village than to risk being swallowed up by the sea monster that was rumored to live in the river. His companion agreed, and they started to leave. As they walked along the beach, the second young man picked up something dark and solid, which turned out to be a human finger bone. They both screamed and ran back to the village, where they told the other villagers about the bone and the monster that must have possessed it. Interpretation
Oral tradition says that this story is about the founding of Ife, one of the oldest cities in Nigeria. The two young hunters are said to be Alamu and Ture, the sons of the king of Egba. According to the story, Alamu and Ture were the first kings of Ife. Some Yoruba scholars identify the "calm" night with the night of the new moon, and the "fog" with the Milky Way. The "sea monster" is probably an alligator, which is common in the Nigerian rivers. The discovery of the human finger bone is said to have been the first sign that the people were no longer in Egulac. The story emphasizes the importance of the gods in Yoruba culture by showing the people seeking the protection of their gods at Ile-Ife.

As they were doing this, the waterfall surged forward and swept away the offering of the two young men. This legend offers several interpretations.  One is that it is a tale of two young men who go to hunt seals and accidentally discover the great waterfall, Whirligig. A young woman came by and they invited her to hunt seals with them. They caught many seals and became very rich. They built a house and lived there with the young woman. One day a big bear came to the house and threatened them. The young woman cooked up a plan. She filled a bucket with water and put it by the side of the house. When the bear came back she opened the door and the bear saw his reflection in the water and became very scared. The bear ran away and never came back. The young woman and the two young men continued to live at the house and hunt seals.

Story analysis
This is a classic tale of a transformative woman who uses her wits to outsmart a dangerous bear. The foggy calm night setting creates a suspenseful atmosphere. The young woman's quick thinking saves the young men from the bear, and her cooking up a plan suggests that she is an intelligent and resourceful character. The triple alliance of the young woman and the two young men is a common motif in native tales. The fact that the young woman was never named is also a common motif in native tales; the story is more about the action than the characters.

Variants
This story is found in many variations among the indigenous peoples of the Pacific Northwest. A Salish tale from the Okanagan nation is similar in many ways, but differs in some important details. In the Salish version, the young woman invites the bear into her house and offers him salmon. While the bear is eating salmon, she ties him up with cedar bark rope. Then she, the two young men, and the old man next door go out and hunt seals. When they return, the young woman feeds the bear more salmon and sends the others to sleep. Once they are asleep, she unties the bear. But the bear is not fooled. He shakes off the ropes and breaks the bowl that the young woman gave him.

The young men were about to return home, when they noticed a strange light in the sky. It was a shooting star, which is a rare sight in the foggy conditions of the north. They made a wish upon seeing the star, and went home happy, forgetting all about the seal hunt.
From that night on, the two young men were no longer troubled by the fear of starvation, as the river provided them with an abundant supply of fish, and they lived comfortably for the rest of their lives. They attributed their good fortune to the shooting star they had seen on that foggy night, and they told their story to many other people, who were also inspired by the stars.
So, in the culture of the Haida people, the shooting star became a source of hope and happiness, and a reminder of the time when two young men from Egulac had their wishes granted by the universe.

Commentary
This story is told by an anonymous narrator to a European ethnologist. The events it relates are said to have happened "a long time ago", but otherwise the story provides no historical context. The characters are typical of legends told by the Tlingit people. Among the Tlingit, the dead are believed to be able to disturb the living if they are not properly cared for. In this story, the spirits of the two hunters are portrayed as troublesome ghosts.

A young woman from Egulac named Wiyuoka was listening to her brother's tale when she heard the tonke again. She told her brother that it was Ishi, the Master of the Tonke, who had laughed at them. His laughter was heard in the foggy night.
Ishi was a trickster figure who played pranks and told riddles. In this story, Ishi is portrayed as a seal, a common target for hunters. The young men from Egulac were probably using torches to light their way, which would explain the calm night despite the fog.

Tonke is a term used in Algonquin languages to refer to a supernatural being or spirit. In this story, Ishi is described as the "Master of the Tonke," suggesting that there may be other tonke out there. The tonke is sometimes personified as a rock or tree, and in this story, it is a creature that can laugh and play pranks.
The story follows a classic pattern of a trickster tale. Ishi, the tonke, creates confusion and laughter among the young men from Egulac. His laughter echoes in the night, adding to the eerie atmosphere created by the fog. The young men are bewildered by their encounter, and Wiyuoka, the young woman listening to the tale, adds to the mystery by explaining that what they heard was Ishi, the Master of the Tonke.
This story shows how the Algonquin people incorporated their environment into their mythology and storytelling. This story is told in several variations by the Algonquian-speaking indigenous peoples of Canada. It is known as the "Girl Who Shot an Arrow", or "The Girl and the Hunter". It is a popular tale among the Mi'kmaq, Passamaquodies, and Penobscots. It is also known as "The Singer of the Sea".
In the Passamaquodie version, the girl's name is not Tsate, but Lana. In the Mi'kmaq version, the girl is named Amahkia. In all versions, the hunters are surprised and impressed by the girl's skills and strength, and invite her to join them.

The twin brothers were hunting for seals near the mouth of the Kootenay River in British Columbia, Canada, when they heard and saw a strange noise. It was 1874.
From their camp on the banks of the Kootenay, Thomas and Thomas-George Tennant heard what sounded like a babble of voices. They shook their heads, thinking it was an illusion brought on by the loneliness. But the sound came again, louder this time, like the rush of many heads against the riverbank.
It was a night for marvels. The full moon rose early and the stars were bright. The twin brothers raced each other to the water's edge and peered into the fog, straining their eyes to see what was making the strange sound.
Suddenly the fog lifted and there, just a stone's throw from the bank, was a village of tall, graceful teepees. The air was filled with the smell of woodsmoke and roasting meat.
The Indians welcomed the brothers and invited them to join in the feast. The Tennants accepted and were entertained all night with music and dancing.
The next day the brothers returned to their camp and prepared to leave. But the villagers called them back, urging them to stay and hunt with them. Thomas and Thomas-George Tennant chose to accept the offer and went back to the village.
For many years after that, the Tennant brothers continued to visit the village by the Kootenay River. And so it was that Thomas married the chief's daughter and Thomas-George married the wife of the tribe's best hunter.

Before they had finished burying the fire pit the sun rose and the fog lifted. As they ran they could hear the cry of the seal in the bag.  When they got to the village they built a new fire pit and cooked the seal, eating it with great relish.  After their meal they laid down to sleep, feeling very satisfied with their hunting skills.  As they slept the seal cried in the bag.
The next day when they woke up the crying had stopped and there was only silence.  The men looked at one another and then opened the bag to see if the seal was gone.  It was gone!  But instead of the expected disappointment, the men felt happy and grateful.  They had provided a meal for their village and had done so with skill and courage. Explanation
This story is told by Tantoo Cardinal in the film "River of Dreams", based on the novel by Tomson Highway. It is a Cree creation story, and relates how the river gave the people its fish, at a time when there were no other foods available. The people were grateful, and honoured the river and its spirits with songs and dances. Then, one day, the river stopped giving its fish freely. The people were hungry, and some of them became angry at the river for withholding its gifts. One young man, Naise, decided to go down to the river to hunt seals, in the hope that he could find other foods. His cousin, Okapi, went with him. They took with them a bag of corn, some tobacco, and a rope.
At the river, they built a fire and cooked some corn. While they were eating, a seal jumped into the fire, and Naise and Okapi realised that they could trap more seals if they worked together. They built a circular wall of stones around a fire, and Okapi went into the water to drive the seals towards the fire while Naise pulled them out of the water with the rope. They shared their meat with the other members of their family, and the Chief was pleased with their

An Ottawa Indian named One-ga-ga-te-ga told them that in such foggy weather the spirits of the dead come out of the river and go back to haunt their people, so they should leave and come again another time. But the two young men were ambitious and they decided to stay and try their luck anyway.
The spirits of the dead appeared and drove the young men back to the shore, threatening to kill them. The young men ran back to the village and reported what had happened.
The next day, the Chief and the Elders decided to go down to the river to hunt seals also. They smoked tobacco and offered gifts to the spirits of the dead, asking them to let them pass.
The spirits allowed them to hunt seals that day, but warned them that if they ever saw them there again, they would turn the waters of the river into scalding hot water, and they would never be able to hunt there again. The young men from Egulac never went down to the river to hunt seals again.

Story Analysis
This is a classicexample of a "warning tale." It tells of the consequences of ignoring the advice of the wise. In this tale, the two young men from Egulac ignore the warnings of One-ga-ga-te-ga and pay the price for their arrogance. The tale also reflects the belief that the spirits of the dead can influence the living.

Story Origin
This tale was told by Shawnee-Delaware Indian leader Tecumseth to American politician Julian S. Smith in the 1830s. Smith recorded the tale in his book, Traditions of the American Indians (1834). The tale has also been told by the Nanticokes, another Iroquoian-speaking group.

The young men were about to give up and make their way back to the village when they heard the sound of a ship's horn in the distance. They looked at each other and decided to swim towards the sound. They managed to get on board the ship before it slipped away from the shore. They sailed with the ship to the Gulf of Mexico, where they were sold into slavery.
One of the young men managed to escape and made his way back to his village, where he told his story to the chief. The chief was very angry that his people had been tricked by the ship's crew and he decided to go to war against the people of Mingan. He chose One Eye, the best warrior of the village, to lead the war party. One Eye took 100 men with him and they set out in three canoes. They sailed through the night and reached Mingan at dawn. The people of Mingan were caught asleep and the village was seized without a fight. One Eye and his men took the women and children hostage and burned the men's town to the ground. They then sailed back to their own village, where they were greeted as heroes. One Eye was particularly celebrated for his bravery and the story of his exploits was told many times over.

The moral of the story is that it is often better to face danger at home than to run from it, and that revenge can be a powerful motivator.

The two young men were hunting seals when suddenly it became foggy and calm. They realized that this was the Time of Silence, a period of stillness and quiet that only occurred every 65 years. The young men put down their weapons and sat quietly on the shore, listening to the gentle lapping of the waves against the shore. They knew that during the Time of Silence, the spirits of the salmon would rise from the ocean to walk the earth for four days before returning to the river to spawn. The young men respectfully greeted the salmon spirits when they appeared, and asked them to continue their journey upriver to the spawning grounds. The salmon spirits agreed, and the young men continued to honor and respect the spirits throughout the Time of Silence.

Teaching Story:
The story of the Time of Silence teaches us about the importance of quiet and stillness in our lives. In a world that is often fast-paced and chaotic, taking the time to sit quietly and listen to the world around us can be a powerful and rejuvenating experience. It also reminds us to respect the cycles of nature and the important roles that silence and stillness play in our lives.

This story is often told in the context of Indigenous Canadian spirituality, but it can be adapted to a wide range of beliefs and practices. For example, in Buddhism, the practice of mindfulness meditation involves sitting quietly and focusing the mind on the present moment in order to achieve a deeper understanding of reality. In Christianity, the story of the Time of Silence could be seen as reflecting the Christian concept of the silent God, who is often described as being beyond human comprehension and who reveals himself to us through the natural world.

Regardless of your belief system, the story of the Time of Silence can serve as a powerful reminder to slow down, be present in the moment, and respect the wisdom of the natural world.

A young woman from Arctic Village came by and joined them in the hunt. They hunted all night but didn't find any seals, and as the sun was rising they saw a large sea otter floating on its back in the water. The young woman  named her otter Kinàgo, and the young men went back to their village empty-handed.
But Kinàgo was not an ordinary otter: when the three of them reached the village, the otter spoke to the chief and the chief's daughter, who were impressed by the otter's beauty and intelligence. The chief's daughter named the otter Kudłàga, which means "fire-making tool" in her language.
For many days the otter lived with the family, helping them in various ways and teaching the young man Kudłići to hunt and fish. Kudłici became a great hunter and farmer, and when he grew up he married the chief's daughter. She gave birth to a son, who was named Gzigojit.
One day Gzigojit went down to the river to hunt seals, and while he was there the tribe's dogs began to bark. Gzigojit followed the dogs and came across a large herd of caribou. He killed as many as he could, and when he returned to the village the chief's daughter suggested that he should go down to the river every year at caribou hunting time.
Gzigojit went down to the river and built a smokehouse, and every year after that the tribe went caribou hunting with him. They never returned empty-handed.

One of the young men, Nootka, was expert in the art of listening. He heaved a sigh and said to his companion, Tonka, "I can hear the heartbeat of the earth."
Tonka rolled his eyes. "You crazy! The earth does not have a heart."
Nootka ignored his friend's scoffing and closed his own eyes. Tonka watched as his friend's shoulders relaxed and his face took on a thoughtful expression.
Nootka opened his eyes and looked at Tonka. "I can hear the heartbeat of the river."
Tonka looked at Nootka, puzzled. "You mean the current?"
Nootka shook his head. "No, I mean the heartbeat of the river. It is slow and strong. Listen!"
Tonka closed his eyes and listened. At first he could only hear the faint sound of water moving over pebbles. But then he heard it - the slow, strong beat of the river's heart.
Nootka smiled. "Now you see?"
Tonka opened his eyes and smiled back. "Yes, I see."
They continued their search for seals, their hearts beating in time with the heart of the river.

Interpretation
This story can be interpreted as an explanation for the full moon. The moon god is called upon to reveal himself and show his power. The young men are ordinary hunters who are unexpectedly witnesses to a divine revelation.

Variants
This story is known in various versions from the Pacific Northwest, told by the Tlingit, Haida, and Salish (Spokane). A similar story is known from the Plains Cree as well. In all versions, the messenger is calling to the chief of the Moon clan.

The moral of the story is that love is demonstrated by actions, in this case waiting for someone to return, and that love is strong enough to overcome Calm and Storm.

Calm and Storm
Calm and Storm is a story that has been passed down through the generations of the Tlingit people. It is a love story that highlights the strength and endurance of love in the face of adversity. The story takes place in the waters surrounding an island in the inlet between Kupreanof and Gadsup Islands, near Sitka, Alaska.

Background
The Tlingit people are one of the Native American tribes of the Pacific Northwest. Their traditional territory includes the coast of Alaska from the Koliganek River on the Alaska Peninsula to the Hubbard Glacier on the mouth of the Chitina River, as well as the inside passages from Puget Sound to the Alsek and Taku Rivers. The Tlingit were an ocean-going people who relied on fishing, hunting, and trading for their survival. They lived in sailing canoes, which allowed them to travel to distant places in search of resources.

The young men were shocked to see the bear, but the bear spoke to them in the Tlingit language, confusing them even more. The bear said, "I am Taku. I live in this river. They heard the distinct barking of seals, but could not see them. They wondered where the seals could be hiding. Suddenly, one of the young men had an idea. "It is said that the seals are prevented from coming to this part of the river by the great snake Ojibway. Maybe if we make a noise like the snake, the seals will think that we are Ojibway and swim closer to us."
They tried this and found that it worked. The seals swam closer and closer until they could easily be speared. The young men speared as many seals as they could in a short time, and then paddled back to their village, where they shared the meat with all the other villagers. And from that time on, the young men from Egulac were known as the seal hunters.

The legend
According to the legend, the great snake Ojibway dwells in the depths of the river. It is said that the snake is there to protect the seals, but sometimes it allows the people of Egulac to hunt them if they show respect to the snake and the river.
The legend is part of the cultural heritage of the Ojibway people. It is told to explain the origin of the annual seal hunt, which is an important social and economic event for the community. The hunt is organized by the Egilk Centre in cooperation with the Canadian Coast Guard and the Mi'kmaq of Gaspé. During the hunt, the community comes together to share in the harvest and to teach the young members of the community about traditional hunting techniques and the importance of respecting the natural world.

A young squaw saw them in the fog and mistook them for spirits, and she ran to tell her father the chief that his spirits had appeared to him.  The chief came down to the river and went on the hunt for these spirits. When he came upon the two young men he killed them and offered their heads as a gift to the spirits of the dead. Commentary
This oral tradition from the Kwakiutl people of the Pacific Northwest shows the importance of spirituality in their daily lives.  It also shows the respect that the Kwakiutl had for the natural world around them.  The fog and calm were not seen as mere weather patterns, but as spiritual entities that could be appeased or offended.  The young men from Egulac were unknowingly the cause of a major event in their community, and their deaths were seen as a gift to the spirits of the dead.  This story illustrates the complex web of beliefs and practices that made up the religion of the Kwakiutl and other Northwest Coast tribes.

From that day on, the Tlingit knew that the earth was round and that the stars were on the sphere itself.

Story analysis
This story is an example of a "star theory" narrative, which is a common motif in the folklore of many cultures. The tale is told in the form of a conversation between two characters, one of whom relates a vision he has had. The vision itself is described in vague terms, and it is left to the audience to interpret the meaning of the stars. In this particular tale, the stars are not holes in the sky, as is commonly believed, but are located on the surface of the Earth, along with the other stars.
