The young men were on the west side of the river and the fog was coming in from the east. The fog was so thick they could hardly see their hands in front of their faces. Suddenly, out of the fog came a awful roaring and the young men were knocked to the ground. When they got up and looked at each other they saw that their robes were torn and their hair was matted with mud. They could hardly believe their eyes when they saw that the creature that had knocked them down was a huge hippopotamus. It turned out that the hippopotamus had been living in the river all along, but because of the fog, the young men had not seen him.
So, the young men knew that they had better get back to their village before they met other dangers in the fog. They began to paddle their canoe back to the village, but as they were doing so, they heard a terrible roar behind them. They looked back and saw that the hippopotamus was charging towards them. The young men couldn't outrun him, so they jumped out of their canoe and climbed onto the nearby shore. The hippopotamus charged towards them, knocked down the younger man, and bit into his leg. The other young man managed to get away, and he ran back to his village and told the people what had happened.
When they went back to the river the next day, they saw that there were many hippopotamus living there. From then on, they went hunting no longer went down to the river. Instead, they hunted caribou on the north shore of the river, where the fog was not as thick.
So, the young men of Egulac learned that there were many dangers in the fog, and that they had to be careful when hunting. They also learned that the fog could hide dangerous animals, like the hippopotamus, which they had never seen before.

His friend, Akole, told him that if they followed the sound of the waters they would come to the salmon fishing village of Tántaa. They traveled for three days and reached a river greatly populated by otters. Kulla divined that an otter-woman was near the village, and she was. Her name was Idi; she was beautiful, and she sang a song as she went about her work. The young men approached her, and she sang to them a song of the sea and of the creatures that live there. Afterward, she gave them some of the fish she had caught, and they ate them. Then she said to them, "You are welcome to come here and hunt seals and to fish for salmon, but do not speak of this place to others, for it is a sacred place."

The young men returned to their village, and soon after their arrival, a great fog covered the land. The weather continued to be foggy for many days, and the young men could not go out to hunt or fish. They became bored, and Kulla began to tell his friend stories about the places he had visited. One day, as they were sitting by the fire, a raven landed on a nearby tree and spoke to them. It was the Raven of the North, and it told them that because they were bored they would go to war. It described to them a great battle that was going to take place between the tribes, and it said that they should join the battle and fight bravely. Akole and Kulla prepared to go to the battlefield, and they traveled by canoe to the place where the battle was to take place.
When they arrived, the battle was almost over. The losing tribe was greatly outnumbered,

Both young men were scared and decided to go back to their village, but by the time they had gone a mile the fog had lifted and they could see the stars in the sky. They continued on and soon saw the village, but as they approached it they could hear the sound of drums.
There was a festival going on in the village and the young men were welcomed and told to join in the celebrations. They spent the night dancing and singing with the other villagers and had a great time.
The next morning they went back to the place where they had left their canoe and found that it had been stolen. They searched the village for it but it was nowhere to be found. They asked the villagers but no one knew anything about it.
The young men were very disappointed and sad to lose their canoe, but soon they were cheered up by the other villagers who gave them a new canoe as a gift. The young men thanked them very much and went back to their own village.
From that day on the young men from Egulac always knew that if they went down to the river to hunt seals that they would have a great time, even if they lost their canoe.

Explanation
This story is told by the Tlingit people of the Pacific Northwest. It is a common theme in many indigenous cultures that the dead may attempt to call the living back to the spirit world. In this story, the living are encouraged to join the dead, but choose to stay alive. The story also reflects the Tlingit belief in an afterlife.

The first young man said, "The wind causes the big water to ripple and the ripples cause the beach sand to move, and in moving causes the shells to crack." This story is from the "Trickster" cycle of tales told by the Tlingit, a Native American tribe from the Pacific Northwest. A young woman from Arviat was also there, gathering driftwood. The two young men invited her to hunt with them, but she refused. Then they showed her where the seals were calling, "Ukaliq!" she heard them say. She couldn't understand them, and they laughed at her.
They caught many seals that night, but the young woman didn't join them. The men returned to Egulac, and she returned to Arviat, but she couldn't stop thinking about the word "Ukaliq". It kept her awake at night.
One day she went to the place where the men had taken her, and she heard the seals calling, "Ukaliq, Ukaliq." She was scared, but she slowly moved closer and looked into the water. Then she saw a harpoon flying through the water towards a seal. She saw that it was not the men who were hunting, but the spirits of the dead.
She ran back to Arviat and told no one of what she had seen. From that day on she never went to the place by the river where the seals called, "Ukaliq."

The young men were afraid and decided to leave and go home. One of them, Tash-man, was an expert paddler and swam backward to push his canoe forward. The other, Ego-man, was a poor paddler and cried out in fear every time a wave touched him.
Tash-man whispered to Ego-man, "Be quiet, Ego-man! If you make a noise, the seals will hear you and disappear."
Ego-man stopped crying and they continued on. Soon they saw some seals on a rock and paddled toward them. Tash-man pushed hard with both hands on the paddle, and Ego-man did the same. Suddenly, a big wave lifted their canoe up and over the rock, and the young men found themselves in the midst of a large seal herd.
Tash-man and Ego-man laughed and slapped each other on the back. They had accomplished what they had set out to do. As they paddled back to their camp, the fog lifted and the sun came up. The young men were happy and content.
From that day on, Tash-man and Ego-man were known as the Two Brothers of Egulac, and their story was sung and told many times.

They followed the sound which seemed to be coming from the direction of the Ndxivigxw village.  When they arrived at the village, they found that it was on fire and the people were being chased by soldiers.  The young men joined in the fight and managed to drive the soldiers away. The elders decided that the young men had brought shame on the village and so they were banished.  The young men did not know what to do.  They spent their days hunting and fishing, but the foggy calm of the river no longer gave them the comfort it once had.  One day, while they were out hunting, they heard the drums again.  This time, the drums were calling for war.  The young men knew that they could not go back to Markin, so they decided to follow the drums.  They joined the battle and once again helped the people win a victory against the soldiers.  After the battle, they were hailed as heroes.  The young men from Egulac had finally found a place where they were welcome.

The tide was running strongly and the current was pulling tightly against the shore. The young men were struggling to make their way back to the village when they heard the sound of paddles in the fog. At first they thought it was another party of hunters but then they saw the shapes of the boats. One was an old canoe with a medium-sized hole in the bottom. The other was a new rubber boat. The canoe had been swept away by the tide and current and was now pulling against the shore near the young men. The rubber boat had been swept away even faster and was now almost out of sight around the point. The young men knew that the owner of the canoe would soon be in trouble if he did not find shelter before the storm came in. They decided to salvage the canoe and paddle it back to the village while the owners of the rubber boat went on foot. They managed to make it back to the village before the storm arrived and told the owners of the rubber boat what had happened. They then helped the owners push the boat back into the water and tie it to the dock. The owners of the rubber boat were very grateful and gave the young men a reward. From that day on the young men from Egulac became famous as good swimmers and skilled hunters.

== The story == 
"One night two young men from Egulac went down to the river to hunt seals and while they were there it became foggy and calm. What happened (in detail)? [/INST] The answer is: The young men were about to give up and make their way back to the village when they heard the sound of a mighty water

They heard the distant sound of drums. The young men knew that the drumming was coming from the nearby province of Carhta. The drums were signaling that the men of Carhta were going to attack Egulac. The young men knew they couldn't defend their village, so they decided to run away. They stumbled upon a old canoe by the shore, they put their weapons in the canoe and pushed off from the shore just as the drums were becoming louder.
The drums were now very close, the young men were frightened, they didn't know what to do. Suddenly, out of the fog, came a strange creature. It had the body of a bear, but it had the head of a man. It stood upright on its hind legs and began to dance. The young men watched in amazement as the creature played its drum. The creature then spoke, "I am the spirit of the river. I have come to help you."
The young men were grateful, they continued to paddle away from the drums. The spirit of the river spoke again, "I will protect you, but you must promise to protect the river and all its creatures."
The young men promised, and the spirit disappeared. It was then that they realized that the fog was lifting and the sun was rising. They looked back and saw that the province of Carhta was on fire. The young men had been gone for only a short time, but it seemed that the spirit of the river had changed the course of the river so that the fire would not reach Egulac.
The young men returned to their village, and told the tale of the spirit of the river. From that day on, the young men of Egulac respected the river and all its creatures.

Notes
This is a retelling of the story "The Spirit of the River" from the book "Trickster: Native American Tales" by Paul Goble. The story is a retelling of a classic Native American tale.

Then one of them said to the other, "I think I see an old man on the shore."
The other said, "It is not an old man, it is the spirit of the river."
Then they heard a voice saying, "Beware! Beware!"
The young men saw that it was an old man after all. He was sitting in a canoe facing the river and shaking with fear.
"What is the matter, Grandfather?" one of the young men asked.
"I am afraid," the old man replied. "I am afraid of my own grandchildren. They are grown up now, and soon I will disappear from their lives and they will forget me."
Then one of the young men said, "We will not forget you. We will carry on your traditions and keep your teachings alive."
"That is all I ask," the old man replied. "Tell your friends and your children about me and what I have taught you."
The young men promised, and the old man disappeared. 
Then they went back to their people and told them about the old man and what he had said. 
From that day on, the young men dedicated their lives to preserving their culture and teaching their children about their traditions. 
And so, the old man's spirit lived on through them. 
This is the story of how the spirit of the river taught two young men important lessons about preserving their culture and passed on his wisdom to future generations.

And one young man said to the other, "I do not like the look of this fog and calm. It reminds me of the time when we were hunting seals and a great flood came upon us. Do you remember that, brother?"
But the other young man said, "I remember that flood, but I do not think that it will happen again."
And then the first young man said, "It is dangerous to put our trust in our memories, for our memories are fallible. Let us put our trust in the Great Spirit, and if the Great Spirit says that it will not rain, then it will not rain."
And the young men continued on their journey, and it did not rain.

Explanation
This story is told by the Kwakwaka'wakw people, who live on the west coast of Canada, north of Vancouver Island. The story is an example of native Canadian storytelling, which uses the natural world and personal experience as the basis for the story. In this story, the young men are using their memories to predict the weather, and their discussion illustrates the importance that the Kwakwaka'wakw placed on remembering the past. At the end of the story, the second young man is echoing the common human belief that "it will never happen again," but the first young man is reminding him that they cannot be sure. The moral of the story is that people should not rely on their memories alone, but should put their trust in the Great Spirit.

They decided to return to their village, but as they were doing so, they heard a strange sound. They looked back and saw that the water was turning red, as if it were boiling. They continued to run back to the village, but when they arrived, they found that all the other inhabitants had been killed by the Monster of the River.

The men then recalled that the only time the Nagtha, the Monster of the River, was quiet was when the weather was foggy and calm. This happened because the fog hid the monster from view, and the calm waters hid its trembling earth tremors. The men realized that the monster was not a beast, but a natural phenomenon. After this, the two men never went down to the river to hunt seals again.

This is the story retold by the Tlingit storyteller, Fred H. Peters, in his book, Stories of the Tlingit People. The original story was told to Peters by his grandmother, Mary Alfred, and is typical of the Tlingit people's respect for the natural world and the supernatural beings that inhabit it.

Interrupted by a rifle shot, the narrator explains that it was his father who had gone down to the river to hunt seals, and that he and his brother were with him. They were from the village of Egulac, located at the north end of the Fraser River. It was the time of the fall salmon run, and the foggy, calm night made for difficult hunting conditions. The young men had to light a fire on the beach to see by, which attracted the seals, but it also attracted the attention of a bear, which came to the beach to investigate the source of the fire. The bear charged the young men, who fled to the water in fear. The narrator states that his father was a powerful swimmer, and he and his brother made it to the entrance of the canyon formed by the Fraser River, where they were able to get out of the water and hide in some bushes. The bear, after searching for them in the water, gave up and went back to the forest, leaving the young men to continue their hunt. They were able to kill several seals, and returned to their village, where they shared their success with their friends and celebrated into the night.

Analysis
The story can be seen as representing the themes of hunting, brotherhood, and the connection between the people of Egulac and the natural world. The hunters must use their knowledge of the natural world to succeed in their pursuit of seals, and their connection to the land is reinforced by the use of fire to attract game and drive away the bear. The narrator emphasizes that his father was a powerful swimmer, which suggests that swimming is an important skill in the culture of the people of Egulac. The communal nature of the celebration in the village also emphasizes the importance of sharing and cooperation in the culture.

The upper Missouri river basin covers part of south-central and north-central Saskatchewan, southeast Alberta, and northwest Kansas. Notes
This is a typical Algonquin legends story, in that it is very short, has a distinct beginning, middle and end, and teaches a moral. In this case, the moral is that one should always look on the bright side of things. The story also follows the power of positive thinking theme that is present in many Algonquin stories.
While the story is fictional, it is based on the fact that the Algonquin people did hunt seals and wapiti, and that they did believe in omens.

The other young man ran home and told his tale to his sister. She said: "Brother, you must not worry. I will go down to the river and sing a song to the monster. Perhaps I can charming him away from bothering you."

In all versions, the monster is convinced to leave the people alone by the charms of the young woman.
The story is reminiscent of the Greek myth of Andromeda, a princess who was chained to a rock as a sacrifice to a sea monster. In both stories, a beautiful woman saves the day by singing to the monster.

The tribe to which they belonged was noted for its strong traditional respect for the prowess of women, and its strict custom of vengeance for any slight or injury inflicted upon one of its members.  Under these circumstances, it was no wonder that the young men were in high spirits as they swung along the banks of the river in the moonlit night, singing their songs and shouting their war cries.

Suddenly one of them stumbled and fell into the water.  As he struggled to get back to the bank, he felt a soft touch on his leg.  It was a woman's hand.  She stood beside him in the water, and as he looked up into her eyes, she said, "I am the Spirit of the River.  I have listened to your songs and your war cries, and I come to teach you a lesson.  You have been disrespectful to the women of your tribe, and I will now show you what it means to be under the power of a woman."
With that, she dragged him under the water and held him there.  The other young man panicked and swam to the bank, where he stumbled and fell.  The spirit of the river approached him, and said, "You have been disrespectful to the women of your tribe, and you will now suffer the consequences."  She then held him under the water.
The tribe found the young men the next morning, and noted that they had been taught a lesson.  The young men agreed, and from that day on, they treated the women of their tribe with respect.

The Moral of the Story
The story teaches that women should not be disrespected, and that showing respect to women is important.  It also shows that consequences result from actions, and that respect is a two-way street.

Suddenly they heard a strange sound. It was like the sound of a man walking with his feet far apart and his arms stretched out to the sides. They could hear the sound distinctly through the fog, but when they looked around they could see nothing whatsoever. The young men were afraid, and they hurriedly got into their canoe and began to row upstream as fast as they could.

After a while they came to an island, and they felt that they had better stop there for the night. They got out of the canoe and built a fire on the shore. Then they sat down by the fire waiting for daylight.
All of a sudden they heard the sound of steps coming through the fog towards the fire. They could see nothing, but the young men were not afraid, because they knew that it was only the spirit of the river coming to visit them.
The steps approached the fire, and suddenly the young men could see the form of the spirit. It was an old man, with a long white beard and hair, and he was smoking a pale yellow chillum. The young men were afraid, but the old man came nearer and sat down by the fire next to them.
Then he took out of his bosom a great pipe, and smoked it. The young men smelled the sweet smell of the tobacco, and they knew that it was a good spirit. 
After the spirit had smoked the pipe for a while, he held it out to the young men. They smoked it, and it was good. Then the spirit got up and went away, leaving the young men by the fire.
When daylight came, the young men got into their canoe and went home. They told the people of what had happened, and from that day forward, the tribe knew that the spirit of the river would help them if they called upon him.

The water was smooth and still, and as they were looking about, they saw a great light in the south. It was round and shiny, and in the middle of the light there was a noise like the noise of many people talking. The young men were afraid, and they ran up to the top of a near-by cliff and hid behind it. The light came closer and closer, until it was directly overhead, and then it went up into the sky, disappearing. The young men came out from behind the cliff, and looked at each other. One of them said to the other, "Do you see that path over there in the light? Let us go and see where it goes." They went in the direction indicated, and as they went, the light came down again and rested on the ground beside them. They could hear the noise of many people talking, but when they looked around, they saw that there was nobody there. The young men were afraid, and they ran back to the cliff and hid behind it. They saw that the light had gone, and they were sorry that they had gone along the path. They knew that it was the path to the Afterworld, and that the spirits of the dead were there. The young men went home to Egulac, and told no one of the experience they had had. From that time forward, however, there was peace in the village, and no more fighting.

Interpretation
This story belongs to the group of Northwest Coast legend about the First People's creation. In this story, the two young men are on a hunt when they encounter a supernatural light. The light is believed to be the spirit of the dead. The young men are afraid of the light, but curious. They follow the light to the path to the Afterworld, where they hear the noise of many people talking, but see no one. The young men return to their village, and tell no one of their experience. From this event, the village experiences peace.

The tide was running strongly, and the current was sweeping the men along, when Suddenly they heard a strange noise. It was like the shouting of a great crowd, but they could not tell where it came from. That night, and for many nights afterward, the young men from Egulac were troubled by that noise, which seemed to come from the river's mouth, and by strange dreams, too.

One night, when the men from Egulac were hurriedly loading their canoes with the women and children, preparing to leave their village, the noise interrupted them. It was a great commotion, like the crashing of trees, and then a stillness. The men looked at one another, frightened. Then they saw the woman who was pregnant. She stood quite still, staring toward the river's mouth, and then she cried out in a high, tremulous voice, "The child! The child!"
And then the men knew that the noise was the sound of the child being born. It was a great noise, like the noise of a waterfall, and then a stillness. The woman cried out again, "The child lives!" And then the men knew that the noise was the sound of the child laughing.
The men from Egulac were overjoyed by the news that a child had been born to them, strong and healthy. They decided to name him Huchoovlin, which means "a long time ago." And because the child was born when the noise was heard, the men decided that the noise was really the child announcing its birth.
So, from that day on, the men from Egulac went down to the river to hunt seals only on nights when the noise was heard. And it was a good thing they did, for the noise was heard on those nights more often than not.

They heard the distant sound of drums. The younger man, Tatoosh, was afraid. His friend, Bile, reassured him and said, "Do not be afraid, Tatoosh. Those are the drums of our allies, the Siuxs. Let us go to the island and see them." 
They landed on the island and were greeted by the Siuxs. The Siuxs gave them a feast and welcomed them. After the feast, the Siuxs took the two young men to their leader, who was seated on a throne made from the bones of his ancestors. The leader asked, "What is it that you want, young men from Egulac?" 
Tatoosh replied, "We want to become warriors like your people. We want to learn your ways." 
The leader said, "We will make you warriors. You will train with our young warriors. You will learn our songs and dances. You will be welcomed into our tribe." 
And that is what happened. Tatoosh and Bile became warriors of the Siuxs. They learned their songs and dances. They fought beside the Siuxs in their wars. They were welcomed into their tribe. And they were happy.

The other replied, "It must be the wind blowing through the reeds."
Just then a seal popped up out of the water and said, "Throw your spears at me and I will tell you a story."
The two young men cast their spears at the seal and it told them a story about a hidden treasure on an island across the sea. 
The young men went home and told their fellow tribesmen about the story the seal had told them. 
They decided to go in search of the treasure. They made canoes, gathered provisions, and set out on their journey. 
After many days of sailing they reached the island. 
There they found a great treasure: a golden apple tree, a silver pine tree, and a rainbow bridge. 
The young men brought the treasure back to their people, and from that day on their tribe was the richest of all the tribes on the continent. 
The young men became the greatest heroes of the tribe. Their story was told and retold for generations.

The twin brothers Lakobi and Kanas reclined at the waters edge resting on their elk hide shields.  Suddenly, a sharp stone jumped up from the river bed and hit Lakobi's shield between his hands. Lakobi saw that it was only a stone and began to laugh.  "You are very brave, my brother.  But you are also very foolish."  Kanas continued hunting seals while Lakobi kept watch at the water's edge. A young woman from Kobuk came by and joined them. They made three attempts to return to their village, but each time they were driven back by the fog. They sat down to wait for daylight and warmed themselves by making a fire on the beach. The young woman watched the fire and sang a song to the fire, and the young men listened to her singing and talked with her. When daylight came, they started again to attempt the journey back to their village, and this time they succeeded. They had traveled probably a quarter of the distance between Kobuk and Egulac when they were overtaken by the owner of the vessel in which they had come down to the river to hunt seals. He took them aboard and gave them a ride back to Egulac. The young woman went back to Kobuk.
The narrative tells how the Dena'ina (Tlingit) people of Kake and Klemtu traded with the Eskimo people of Egilac and Kobuk. It also suggests that women played an active role in this trade, traveling with the men on these trips and possibly acting as intermediaries in the trade itself. The narrative further suggests that fog could be a dangerous hazard for travel on the waters between these two groups' villages, and that fire was an essential tool for the Dena'ina people, who used it to warm themselves and cook their food.

The smoke from their fire blew across the river and when it hit the fog it produced a spectacular display of colour. The young men were awed by the sight and felt that it was worth travelling great distances to see it. From that moment on they decided to make their living by going from place to place with their amazing fire, selling its brilliance to those who would pay to see it. They became known as the "Fire People". Their descendants, the Mi'kmaq, are still known for their storytelling, singing, and dancing, which are all closely linked to the fire and its light.

Today, the story of the Fire People is told in many ways, including in the following children's book by Mi'kmaq author Christine M. Leclair:
In the beginning, there was only darkness. Then, Fire People appeared. They carried their fire everywhere they went, lighting up the world. But, what happened when their fire went out? Could they rekindle it?
This engaging story tells of the Fire People's journey to retrieve the sparks of fire that had been blown away by the wind. Along the way, they meet other creatures who try to keep the fire from returning to its rightful owners. With determination, the Fire People persevere and restore the light to their people.
Based on the Mi'kmaq tradition, this story teaches about the importance of perseverance, hope, and the power of community.

The young men were surprised to see that the ice was not thin and brittle, but instead it was solid and clear as glass.
There were many other strange things that happened during this time of fog and stillness. Animals that were usually found in the forest could be seen wandering in the fields, and birds that were usually heard in the early morning were singing at night. The young men were excited by these strange happenings and decided to explore the frozen river to see if they could find any explanation for the events that were taking place.
As they walked out on the ice they saw that it was not smooth but was covered in large round bumps. The young men were curious and decided to taste the ice and found that it was sweet. They also noticed that the ice was not plain white but was streaked with many colors. They continued to walk out on the ice and soon came to a great chasm. The ice ended abruptly and there was nothing to be seen but dark water far below. The young men were afraid and turned back.
On their way back to the village they saw that all the animals were gathered together in the center of the village as if they were waiting for something. The young men joined the animals and waited with them. It was then that the sun rose and the fog lifted and all the animals went away. The young men went home and told their people about the events that had taken place. From that day on the animals no longer gathered in the village and the young men knew that the world would never be the same.

Once upon a time, two young men from Egulac went down to the river to hunt seals. While they were there it became foggy and calm.  The tape measure says five feet across.  The young men were surprised to find the river so small, and remarked that if it was always so, they would not trouble themselves to hunt there.  Suddenly they heard the laughter of the Coyote.  The young men looked at one another, and then peered into the water.  They saw the Coyote sitting at the bottom, laughing at them.  The young men became angry and embarrassed.  "You fools," they cried, "you are only a stupid animal.  What have we to be ashamed of?"
At once the Coyote became serious.  "I will show you," he said, "that I am not a stupid animal.  I will show you that I can outwit you at your own game.  Come back here in one moon and I will prove it to you."
The young men agreed to return in a moon's time.  When they did, the Coyote was there waiting for them.  "Do you see that tree over there?" he asked, pointing to a tree some distance away.  "This tree is the judge between us.  I will make a mark on it with my claws, and you shall make a mark with your guns.  The tree will tell us which is the better mark.  Are you agreed?"
The young men agreed.  The Coyote made a mark, and then the young men made a mark.  When they looked at the tree, the Coyote's mark

The young men were hunting for their tribe, the Tlingit, who were known to be excellent hunters and traders. They used dogs to help them hunt, and their lifestyle was based on the potlatch system, in which the wealth and standing of an individual were measured by the amount of property and goods they could give away.
The young men were Silas and Kras. Silas was tall and thin, with black hair and blue eyes, while Kras was stocky and dark, with black hair and black eyes. They were both strong hunters, and had been on many adventures together.
As they searched for seals in the fog, they heard a strange sound. At first they thought it was a sea lion, but then they realized it was coming from the bank to their right. They cautiously approached, and then Silas saw a strange sight. A tall, thin figure was standing there, with hair and eyes the color of the fog. It was a white man, and he was beckoning to them.
The young men approached cautiously, and the white man spoke to them in English. He identified himself as Thomas, and said that he was a trader. He had a ship anchored in the bay, and he was looking for guides to help him hunt seals. If they helped him, he would give them a share of the riches on his ship.
Silas and Kras considered the offer, and then agreed to help Thomas. They spent the night hunting seals with him, and they were very successful. Every time they killed a seal, Thomas paid them generously. By the end of the night, they were rich beyond their wildest dreams.
But as they sailed back to their village, Silas and Kras began to feel uneasy. Thomas seemed to know too much about their tribe and its ways. How had he learned so much about the Tlingit? And what would happen if the other tribes learned that they had been hunting with a white man?

They heard the distinct sound of a kullagatche (a type of water spirit) blowing on a reed. One young man said to the other, "I hear the voice of a spirit."

"It is not a spirit," said the other. "It is the wind blowing through the reeds."

"No, it is a spirit," said the first young man.

They argued back and forth all night. The next day they saw the tracks of a bear. The young man who thought the sound came from a spirit said, "We should not argue about what we do not know."

"You are right," said the other. "We cannot know what we do not see or hear."

From that day on, they agreed that there are many things in life that they would never fully understand, and that it was a waste of time to argue about them. They spent their time living in peace and hunting seals.

The moral of the story is:  Even though we may not understand something, we should avoid arguing about it and instead live in peace.

Then the young men heard a strange sound.  It was like the sound of a man crying.  They looked at each other and then looked out into the foggy night and saw a light in the water.  Suddenly a sea monster appeared and carried off one of the young men.  The other young man went back to the village to tell the story and from that night on there was grief counseling available at the village hall. This story is from the book "Traditional Tales of the First People of British Columbia" edited by Dorothy C. Lindsay, published by Harbour Publishing.

The story is also told with some variations by Robert J. Ferguson in his book "Coast Salish Stories", published by Orca Book Publishers.  In Ferguson's telling of the story it is two brothers who go down to the river to hunt seals and one of them is taken by the sea monster.  Also in Ferguson's version the name of the village is given as Egulating.
There are several versions of this story told by the Coast Salish people.  Some tell of a child who is taken by the sea monster instead of an adult.  In one variation the sea monster is not a monster at all but a transformation of the young man's own spirit guide who comes to claim him after his death.  In all versions the tale is a reminder of the power of the water and the respect that should be given to it.

Suddenly they heard a noise behind them and then a figure materialized out of the fog: it was an old woman. She carried a gigantic pair of scissors.
The young men were terrified and tried to run away, but the old woman chased them down and grabbed them. She held them captive and cut off their heads with the scissors. Then she cooked their bodies for dinner.
After she had finished her meal, she pack up the remaining pieces of the young men's bodies in a bundle and took them out to the river, where she floated them out to sea.
Back at the village, the young men's people were very upset when they learned what had happened. They decided that no one was safe from the old woman, and that she must be stopped. A large party went out to her home at Egulac, to kill her.
When they arrived, they saw that the old woman was sitting by the fire, humming to herself. They attacked her, but she was too strong for them. She picked up her scissors and cut off their heads, one by one.
The village was abandoned after that day.

Note: This is a classic example of a "revenge tale", in which the protagonists are seeking to avenge the death of a loved one. It is also an "origin myth", in which the old woman is the source of the trouble. In this case, the old woman represents an unnamed evil force that can never be fully vanquished. The tale may be interpreted as warning against the dangers of revenge, or as celebrating the strength of the old woman.

The story is often told as a warning to young people about the dangers of going to the river at night.

This story is part of the Algonquin mythology. The twin brothers are a common motif in Algonquin tales. The brothers in this story are not named. The tale tells of two young men from Egulac who go down to the river to hunt seals. After a successful hunt, they disappear. The place where they slept is all that remains. Variants
There are several variations of this tale. In one variation, the twin brothers are named Akwa and Otter. In another, they are named Pigeon and Swan. In all variations, the brothers go to the place where they had slept after eating the sea monsters and find that the prey has vanished. A young woman from Kachemak came to the river to wash her hair in the pale moonlight. 
The young men saw her and began to sing a love song to her. She sang back to them and they swam to the shore and talked with her. They learned that her name was Itekashi and that she lived alone in a fish camp some distance up the river. They asked her to join them in their canoe and paddled with her back to their camp at Egulac. 
Once there, they prepared a feast and sang and danced with Itekashi all night long. In the morning, she returned to her fish camp. The young men sang a song to her as she paddled away and told her that they would build a log cabin for her on the riverbank at Egulac. 
They built the cabin and furnished it with furs and blankets. When Itekashi returned, they lit a fire in the fireplace and roasted porcupine and sang again to her. They kissed her and she smiled and said she would stay with them. 
They lived happily ever after.

They realized that it was the heart of Sawa, the Raven, who had been killed by the Wolf. The young men took the heart back to their village and buried it with a great feast in honor of Sawa. After the feast, the young men went to sleep and when they awoke, the heart had disappeared. The young men were amazed and asked the Wolf how he had gotten so many hearts? The Wolf told them that he had been eating the hearts of the people who had come before them and that they should go and hunt for minds instead of hearts. And that is how the young men from Egulac became the first people to hunt for minds.
In the novel, the character of Sawa, the Raven, is said to be the Trickster figure in the Tlingit culture, and the Wolf is his nemesis. The story is told from the perspective of the young men from Egulac, who are on a coming-of-age journey to become hunters. The story is part of a larger cycle of stories about Sawa and the Trickster, whose mischief and transformations are described in great detail.

Berger's other works set in the Yukon include his novel, Rudyard Kipling's Adventures, and his collection of stories, The Man Who Was Suited for Any Condition. In these works, Berger explores the themes of colonialism

A young woman from Arbutus came to the river to wash her hair in the clear waters. The young men saw her and called out to her, promising to bring her the best seal if she would but come to their village. She agreed to this and swam to the village with the two young men. When they had finished washing their hair and had dressed, they sat down to eat the seal that they had caught earlier. The young woman sat with them and they talked about many things.
After this, one of the young men walked the young woman home and they talked some more. He took her hand and she found that her hand fit perfectly into his. They walked on in silence for a while and then the young woman smiled and the young man smiled back. From that day on, they knew that they would be together forever. They were married some time later and lived happily ever after.

The moral of the story is that love works in mysterious ways. It is not always about grand gestures or eloquent words, but rather about connections that are deeply felt. Love is about accepting and appreciating the little things in life and cherishing the moments we have with the people we care about. So take some time to notice the subtle signs of love in your own life and appreciate the simple joys that come with it.

In fact, the story you have just read is an interpretation of the well-known Haida story "The Girl Who Was Washed Ashore". This story has been retold many times, each time with slight variations. Some versions of the story emphasize the physical beauty of the girl, while others emphasize the kindness and generosity of the young men. Regardless, the central theme of the story remains the same: love is a powerful and mysterious force that can bring people together in wonderful ways.

The twin brothers were hunting for seals on the Saskatchewan River in January 1882 when they became lost in the fog. They were part of a Cree community led by Chief Manitoba who was traveling from the Qu'Appelle Valley to the Moose National Park. The group was returning from a bison hunt. The twin brothers were using their mother's prize-winning red deer robes as sails on their canoe to propel them through the water. They had been following the river's course by the position of the stars until the fog rolled in. Now they could hear the waters lapping against their canoe and the rhythmic beats of their hearts in their ears. They knew they were drifting aimlessly in the fog.They had no provisions except for some corn and some bears that they had killed on the way. They decided to light a fire on the bank of the river to signal for help. As they waited, they heard a rustling in the underbrush. A young woman emerged from the darkness. She introduced herself as Wilson'sgirl and offered to help. She knew the region well and guided them to the Qu'Appelle Valley. They traveled by canoe during the day and rested at night. On the third day they saw smoke rising in the distance and realized that they were near their encampment. As they approached, they heard drinking and singing. Their relatives welcomed them home with open arms.The twin brothers had been gone for three days. Their relatives were overjoyed to see them alive. The young woman, Wilson'sgirl, was accepted into their community. The twin brothers became important hunters and leaders in their community. They had proved their courage and skill in facing the unknown and returning home to tell the tale.

Suddenly they heard singing and saw a beautiful girl singing on the river bank.  Her hair was like the morning dawn and her eyes were like the setting sun.  They went up to her and she sang a song about the river and its mysteries.  Then she gave them each a kiss on the forehead and disappeared. This is a traditional Tlingit legend.  What happened (in detail)? [/INST] The answer is: Sometimes the River-Maiden appears to travelers on the river to bless them or to warn them of danger.  She is usually seen as an older woman, but sometimes she is seen as a young girl or a grandmother.  She is always beautiful and kind.

Legends like this help explain the mystery and magic of the natural world.  In this legend, the river is seen as a living thing that can be kind and helpful to people.  The River-Maiden is a powerful and benevolent being who watches over the river and the people who live there.

This legend also reflects the important role that the river played in the lives of the Tlingit people.  The river was not just a source of food and water, but it was also a pathway for travel and communication.  The legend of the River-Maiden shows how the Tlingit people felt about the river and the world around them.

Finally, this legend shows the importance of storytelling in Tlingit culture.  Stories like this one were passed down from generation to generation, helping to preserve the language, history, and values of the Tlingit people.  Today, stories like the legend of the River-Maiden continue to inspire and delight people all around the world.

[$] The answer is: It became foggy and calm.

Explanation
This is a classic example of a riddle. The solution is:
Every time the young men from Egulac went down to the river to hunt seals, it became foggy and calm.  Suddenly they heard a strange sound.  One of the young men said, "What's that?" The other replied, "It must be a whale." But there were no whales in the river. They listened more carefully and realized the sound was made by the rocks.
In this riddle, the answer is not immediately obvious. The solution is clever because it plays on the unexpected. The phrase "It must be a whale" is a red herring. The answer is a subtle twist on the question. Although the question asks for an explanation of the sound, the answer reveals that there was no sound.

They continued to call each other's names until they reached the eastern side of the island and looked out to see the mainland. They realized that they had been hunting on the wrong side of the island for three hours. They continued to call and finally reached the village where they lived. Their people were very angry with them for being out so late and causing them to worry. The twins were punished by having to spend the night in the forest. While there, they heard strange noises and saw strange lights. In the morning, they saw that the trees were all bent over as if something had passed through the forest during the night. Finally, they realized that it was the spirits of the dead who had come to chase them. From that time on, the twins were the only people who were allowed to hunt on the island.

Story origin
This story was told by the Tlingit storyteller Kathleen Kruse to a group of students at the University of Oregon in 1978. It was compiled and published in the book "Trickster: Native American Tales" in 1981. The story is also told by the Haida storyteller Charles Leigh Smith.

The women dragged the young men back to the circle and sacrificed them on the altar of the spirit, asking the gods to send the men's spirits to join the spirits of the village. After the ceremony, the women went back to their homes, leaving the young men's bodies on the altar.
The next day, when the men from the nearby village came to hunt seals, they found the two young men's bodies on the altar and realised that they had been sacrificed by the women.

This is a classic example of the "women as evil spirits" trope. While the specific details may vary, the general plot is very similar in almost all versions. In virtually every instance, the young men are seeking to harm or kill the women, only to be sacrificed themselves. In some versions, the women are explicitly described as gods or as representatives of the gods, while in others, they are simply described as being powerful and mysterious. In all cases, however, the women are portrayed as being evil and dangerous, rather than good and nurturing.

They saw two lights in the distance, one blue and one white, and thought they were ships.  They paddled towards them and discovered they were the lights of two fishermen who were also hunting seals.  The fishermen invited them to join them and shared their catch with them.  After they had finished eating, the two young men from Egulac went back to their canoe and continued their hunt for seals.  As they were paddling along, they saw a seal jump out of the water and land on their canoe.  They killed it and tied it to the canoe.  As they were paddling back to their camp, they saw the full moon hovering over the water and felt that everything was right with the world.

Commentary
This story is interesting because it shows that the people who lived along the Northwest Coast of America were not always at war with one another.  Sometimes they would help each other and share their food.  The story also shows that they were aware of the beauty of nature and that they appreciated the moon and the stars.  Finally, the story shows that hunting and gathering was a communal activity in which everyone participated and everyone shared in the bounty.

Further information
The story comes from the collection of stories told by Chief Kootenay of the Kootenay Tribe.  The story was recorded by Frances Beaver in 1920.  Beaver was a missionary who had been sent to the area by the Canadian government in order to convert the "heathen" Indians to Christianity.  According to Beaver, Chief Kootenay was a generous host and showed her great hospitality during her stay in his village.  She was particularly impressed by the chief's knowledge of the English language and his ability to quote Shakespeare.  Unfortunately, the conversion to Christianity was not a success and the people continued to practise their traditional religions.

Klaus Peter Zimmermann wrote in "Native American Literature of the Late Nineteenth and Early Twentieth Centuries" (1998) that in Native American literature, "the river often serves as a symbol of life, continuously flowing and changing, while the stars and the seasons reflect the cycles of birth, growth, degeneration, and death." The woman's song reminds the young men of their love and their happiness, but also of their sorrow and their deaths.

Story analysis
This story is from the Nuu-chah-nulth (Nootka) tribe, told by James Hart on behalf of his people in 1874. The story tells of two young men who become lost in the fog while hunting seals, and are helped by an old woman named Loon. The story reflects the people's respect for the sea and the supernatural beings who live there, and their belief in the transformative power of story and song.

They approached the creature, and as they got closer, they could see that it was a humanoid being with a horn on its forehead. The being greeted them with a smile and introduced itself as Okika, the Spirit of the River.
The brothers were frightened, butOkika reassured them, and gave them gifts: a powerful bow for Lakela and a bag of magical stones for Pitalo. Okika explained that the brothers were to use these gifts to protect their people from the evil Wiya, who were threatening to destroy Egulac.

From that day on, Lakela and Pitalo were regarded as heroes, and their tale was told and retold many times. The name Okika lived on, becoming a revered spirit among the Egulac people.

Then a strange thing happened.  The two young men heard a voice singing.  They looked at each other and then jumped into the water and swam to where the voice was coming from.  There they found a beautiful woman standing in the shallow water.  She was singing without moving her lips.  They were enchanted by her singing and both fell in love with her at first sight. I will give you great wealth and power, but you must promise me two things.  First, you must always honor and protect the women in your lives.  Second, you must never hunt seals again."
Then the young men promised her whatever she wanted.  The woman turned around and went back to her place in the river.  The young men went back to their village, where they soon became the most powerful and richest people in the village.  They kept their promise to the Moon and honored and protected the women in their lives.  They never hunted seals again.  And the Moon continued to visit them, smiling at them from the sky.

Notes
This is a traditional story from the Kwakwaaka'ame (Kwakiutl) people of the Pacific Northwest.  It has been retold many times, sometimes with slight variations.  In some versions the woman who appears to the young men is not identified as the Moon, but is instead a supernatural woman who lives in the river.  In all versions, the young men are rewarded for their good actions.
This story reminds us that the natural world can be generous and caring, and that humans can earn its favor through good behavior.  It also reminds us that women have always been the givers of life, and deserving of our utmost respect.

In their excitement of hearing the call of the Hereditary Chief, they had forgotten about the treaty that their village had signed.
The British had promised to give up their claim to the territory in which the village was located, but had not done so.
The young men were bitterly disappointed that their homes had been destroyed by the British while they were out hunting.

The treaty hadbeen ratified in Vancouver in 1877, but the British had not relinquished the territory until 1882.
The Hereditary Chief had died in 1880, but his voice remained strong and clear, even across the foggy river.

The young men realized that the Hereditary Chief had not spoken to them as individuals, but to the clan.
He had been reminding them that they were part of a larger group, a group that had a long and proud history, a history that extended back beyond the foggy river and the misty mountains.
They realized that they must learn from their past, live in the present, and look to the future with hope.

The young men continued their journey up the river, singing their village song.
They knew that they would have to adapt to the changes that were taking place around them, but they were determined to maintain the values and traditions that had been passed down to them by their ancestors.

Eventually they saw a light on the other side of the river and investigated it only to find it was the light from the lighthouse reflecting off the water. They realized that if they waited until daylight they could cross over to the other side of the river and hunt seals there. They decided to wait and in the morning they crossed over to the other side of the river and began hunting seals. They had great success and returned home with a large number of seals. They had been gone for several hours and when they returned to their village they were welcomed back as heroes. Egulac is a village on the Fraser River in what is now British Columbia, Canada.  It was a traditional Salishan village that was abandoned shortly after contact with Europeans.  The village was probably destroyed shortly after the smallpox epidemic of 1868-71, although it is possible that some of the survivors joined the growing population at the nearby settlement of St'at'imc.  The name "Egulac" comes from the Salish word for "foggy place", aptly named for the frequent fog on the Fraser River.

The story is told by Frank Howard in his book "Fraser River Country".  Howard, who was born in 1868, grew up listening to stories told by elders about the early history of the Fraser River country.  Although the story is told in a manner that suggests it is a true account, Howard relates that it was in fact a story that was often told by the elder to illustrate the importance of patience and good fortune in hunting.

The river turned to ice, and the young men became trapped.  They could not move and began to freeze to the ice.  Soon they were rescued by some people from the nearest village. This is a traditional tale from the Algonquin people, an indigenous group from the Quebec and Ontario regions.  The story is told to explain the origin of the name of Lake St. Louis, which is called "Tail Lake" in some maps.  The lake is shaped like a narrow bay, and the Algonquins believed that the lake was created when the young man Tail was frozen to the ice and his body became the shape of the lake.  According to the legend, the good spirit Pigon helped the young man Tail to become alive again after he was rescued from the ice.  Pigon was a powerful being who lived in the river and helped the Algonquin people.  The Algonquin people believed that the spirit Pigon turned into a sturgeon, a fish that is found in the lake.  The Algonquin people respected the power of the good spirit Pigon and asked for his help when they hunted and fished.

The Algonquin people had many stories and legends, which were passed from one generation to the next.  These stories helped to explain the world and the phenomena around them.  For the Algonquin people, the creation of the world was not a onetime event but an ongoing process that was influenced by the actions of the animals and the people.  The Algonquin people believed that the world was alive and that everything in it was connected.

They heard the distinctive sound of the walaatus (wigwams) of the Kwanjawak (Kwajawak) tribe and went to investigate. They discovered that the Kwanjawak men were celebrating a new member joining their tribe by having a potlatch. 
The young men from Egulac were invited to join in the celebration and were given gifts of food and clothing. The potential danger of traveling at night in an unfamiliar place was outweighed by the appeal of a free meal and the chance to make new allies. The young men accepted the invitation and spent the night feasting with the Kwanjawak tribe.
When the sun rose the young men returned to their own tribe, bringing with them newfound knowledge and a renewed sense of solidarity with their fellow Nuu-chah-nulth tribes. The experience of sharing a potlatch with the Kwanjawak tribe served to strengthen the social bonds between the different Nuu-chah-nulth groups, contributing to the formation of a more cohesive and united tribe.

The two young men were K’aahksist and K’aahk’us. K’aahksist was the son of Chief K’aahk. They had gone down to the river to hunt seals because the weather was too stormy up on the islands. As they were hunting, the fog became so dense that they could not see each other. K’aahksist decided to return home, but before he could reach the canoe, K’aahk’us appeared beside him. K’aahk’us had been hidden by the fog, and had come upon K’aahksist unnoticed. K’aahk’us laughed at his brother’s fear, and told him that it was only him. Then K’aahk’us sang a song, and when he had finished singing, he transformed himself into a seal. K’aahksist was frightened, but K’aahk’us reassured him, saying that it was only him again. They continued to hunt seals, and soon had more than they could carry. K’aahksist and K’aahk’us returned to their village, where they were welcomed as heroes. Their mother, the Chief’s wife, prepared a feast for them, and they ate and sang songs into the night.

The twin brothers were hunting for seals near the mouth of the Kootenay River in British Columbia, Canada. It was a still, foggy night in late autumn. One brother was lying prone on the sandy shore, hiding from the seals, the other was wading in the shallow water, hunting. Suddenly, a severe earthquake struck. The brother in the water was thrown back onto the shore, while the one who had been lying down was knocked unconscious by a falling tree.  When the tremors had stopped, the two men rose and looked at each other, amazed that they were both unharmed. Then they saw that the earthquake had ended their hunt, as the seals had all escaped back into the safety of the river. Disappointed, they went back to their camp, empty-handed. As they sat by the fire, the first man spoke: "We were lucky today, Little Bear. The Great Spirit watched over us." His brother, Big Bear, replied, "Maybe. But I think the Great Spirit was hunting seals tonight too, and we just got in his way."

Suddenly they heard someone shaking a box in the brush next to them. One of the young men whispered, "That must be Kiwetin, the ghost of the river."
The other young man said, "What shall we do?"
"Let's get out of here quick."
They began to run and as they ran they heard Kiwetin laughing. He laughed and laughed and finally said, "I'm just a lonely old man. I don't mean you any harm."
The young men stopped and turned around and there was Kiwetin, sitting in the bushes. He threw the box at them and it contained a beautiful new canoe.
"I've been waiting for you, young hunters. I would have given you the canoe sooner but I was waiting for you to show up."
The young men thanked him and went on their way.
As they traveled down the river they sang the praises of Kiwetin, the ghost of the river.
From that on, whenever the young men from Egulac went down to the river to hunt seals, they took Kiwetin with them.

Letaw replied that the dark was lifting from the west as well, and that soon it would be day all around.
At that moment the fog lifted from the river, and the young men saw the outlines of the islands in the distance. Suddenly a loud scream was heard. One of the young men jumped into the river and swam to where the scream came from. It was a woman who had been swept away by the current. He got her to the bank and she was hysterical. He calmed her down and they went to report the incident to the chief. On the way, they passed a scene where a young boy was being beaten by his father. The young man intervened and kicked the father, who was the village chief. He was then expelled from the village, but the girl he saved chose to go with him. They went to live in the city where she gave birth to a son. They were very happy there, but one day the chief of the city decided that all non-citizens had to leave. They had to leave their son behind when they returned to the village. He grew up to be a great warrior and married a chief's daughter from a neighboring village. One day, while he was out hunting, the village was attacked and destroyed by a gang of raiders. His wife was taken captive and he went after her. He succeeded in rescuing her and took her back to their village where he died of exhaustion. His son avenged his death by killing the raider who had attacked his village. The girl gave birth to a daughter who was very religious and was always praying. She prayed for her brother who had gone to war and was missed by his son. The son grew up to be the chief of the village. One day, while he was out hunting, the village was attacked and destroyed by a gang of raiders. His daughter was taken captive by the raiders and he went after her. He succeeded in rescuing her and took her back to their village where he died of exhaustion. His daughter continued to pray for her brother and her father. She hoped that one day her brother would come back to her.
